content.content: 1 # Ripul website 2 3 The public site at **https://app.ripul.io**: what Ripul is, who it is for, and how to get it. It is separate from the app, which lives at `demo.ripul.io` (`chrome-extension/`). 4 5 Plain HTML and CSS with one small script. No build step and no dependencies. 6 7 ``` 8 public/ 9 index.html home 10 download/index.html the Mac downloads, and how to be invited to the iPhone app on TestFlight 11 start/index.html getting started: install, sign in, first conversation 12 features/ one page per feature, and an index — GENERATED, see below 13 library/ the Ripul Library: catalogue and listings (one page; see below) 14 js/library.js the library's script — GENERATED from src/library.ts 15 help/ the help guides — GENERATED, see below 16 js/help.js the guides' script — GENERATED 17 images/ screenshots used by the guides 18 story/index.html the founder's story 19 404.html 20 css/site.css one stylesheet for every page 21 js/site.js top-bar hairline and arrive-on-scroll 22 fonts/ Instrument Serif and Archivo (both SIL Open Font Licence), served from here 23 img/ 24 ``` 25 26 ## Feature pages 27 28 Every feature section on the home page ends in a "Learn more" link to a page under `/features/`. Those pages share one layout, so they are written by `tools/features.py` from the `FEATURES` list at its top. To change one, edit the list and run `python3 website/tools/features.py`, then commit the pages it writes. Do not edit `public/features/` by hand. A section in that list can end with screen grabs of the app (source, size, alt text, caption); a tall one is shown in a phone frame. Keep the image files in `public/images/`, and look at every grab for private names or conversations before it goes in: this is a public site. A feature can also open with a `story`: numbered steps, each a paragraph above a large recording (see "Yours to keep"). Recordings never start by themselves: the visitor presses play (Peter, 8 October 2026). They show a poster picture until then, and follow the Video section below for where the files live. A new feature section on the home page needs an entry in that list and a `Learn more` in its copy. Nothing else on the site is generated. 29 30 ## The Ripul Library 31 32 The public library of artefacts is part of this site: `/library` is the catalogue and `/library/` is one listing, opened and run in place. Until 9 October 2026 it was a page of the web app at `demo.ripul.io/library`; that address now sends people here. What the library is, and its rules, are in `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/artefactLibrary.md`. 33 34 - **One page, two views.** Both addresses are `public/library/index.html` (`public/_redirects` rewrites `/library/*` to it) and `js/library.js` reads the address. Where a path cannot be rewritten, `/library/?open=` opens the same listing. 35 - **The script is built, not written in place.** Its source is `src/library.ts`; `bash website/tools/library.sh` type-checks it and writes `public/js/library.js`. Commit what it writes. 36 - **The sandbox is the app's, not a copy.** The document a web artefact runs in, and the checks on what it may send, are imported from `chrome-extension/` (`webDocument.ts`, `webArtefactContract.ts`, `artefactRuntime.ts`). So rebuild the script when those change, and never re-implement them here. 37 - **A visitor has no account.** The page sends no credentials and calls the worker's anonymous routes directly (`llm-proxy.ripul.io/v1/public/library`), so the per-address run limit sees the visitor. The worker already allows this origin. 38 - **Everything a user wrote goes in as text.** Titles, summaries and author names are never inserted as markup. 39 - **Not indexed** (`_headers` and the page's own robots tag), because nobody has decided whether user-written listings should be searchable under Ripul's name. 40 - **Proof:** `node website/tests/library-proof.mjs` drives the pages in Chromium and WebKit against a local stand-in (`tests/library-standin.py`): browse, search, open, run a calculator, run a web artefact through the sandbox, report, and check the frame can reach neither the site nor the network. 41 42 ## Help guides 43 44 The help guides are pages of this site (`/help/`), and they are also what the apps show in their Help sheet. Their words live in one place, `content/helpContent.ts`: typed blocks, not Markdown, with the house style at the top of the file. `tools/help.ts` turns that into `public/help/` and `public/js/help.js`. To add or change a guide, edit the content file, then from the repository root run 45 46 ```bash 47 chrome-extension/node_modules/.bin/tsx website/tools/help.ts 48 ``` 49 50 commit what it writes, and deploy the site. No app rebuild is needed: the sheet loads the pages live. 51 52 What the apps rely on, so do not break it: 53 54 - **Addresses.** A guide is `/help//`. The sheet asks by hash, `/help/#/help/` or `/help/#/help/screen/` (the guide for an app screen, from the `screens` list on each article); `help.js` reads the hash and goes to the page. 55 - **The conversation with the sheet.** `help.js` tells the sheet the guide's id and title (`ripulHelp` messages), answers its back button (`window.__ripulHelpBack`), and hands any link that is not a guide back to the sheet to open outside. In a browser all of that does nothing. 56 - **Appearance.** In the sheet the site's header and footer are hidden (`.in-sheet`) and `?theme=dark` turns on the dark palette (`.theme-dark` in `css/site.css`). The sheet paints the same page colour behind the web view (`HelpCenterSheet.swift`, `backgroundColor`); change the two together. 57 58 ## Video 59 60 Do not put video files in `public/`. The site's static hosting answers every request with the whole file and ignores requests for part of one, and Safari will not play a video served that way (measured 8 October 2026). Video lives in the `ripul-builds` storage bucket under `downloads/site-video/` and is served, in parts, from `https://demo.ripul.io/dl/site-video/`. Upload with 61 62 ```bash 63 cd chrome-extension 64 CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=48994301be053cfc75d066dfaed15e35 npx wrangler r2 object put ripul-builds/downloads/site-video/ --file --content-type video/mp4 --remote 65 ``` 66 67 To make a clip from a simulator recording: cut the still stretches with `tools/gapcut.swift` (it compares frames, so a spinner does not count as movement), then re-encode with ffmpeg, which is what makes it small. A 48-second Duo recording went from 33 MB to 1.7 MB with no visible loss: 68 69 ```bash 70 swiftc -O website/tools/gapcut.swift -o /tmp/gapcut 71 /tmp/gapcut take.mov cut.mp4 1.5 1.0 0.002 # stills over 1.5s cut to 1s 72 ffmpeg -i cut.mp4 -an -vf "scale=1280:-2,fps=30" -c:v libx264 -preset slow -crf 26 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart clip.mp4 73 ``` 74 75 `/test/duo-video/` is an unlinked test page that plays one such recording. 76 77 ## Identity 78 79 The site takes its type and logo from the brand identity chosen on 8 October 2026 ("Option 01"), but **not its colours**. Peter's decision that day: keep the site's own warm palette (paper, navy, teal, with coral and gold accents), and let the identity's deep green `#2d4829` and lime `#aef572` appear only as very rare dashes. 80 81 - **Type:** Instrument Serif for headlines and the wordmark (one weight only, so never ask for a bold), Archivo for everything else. 82 - **The mark:** the dot of the "i" in Ripul, cut by a slanted line. It is one SVG path, redrawn by eye from the brand sheet (`img/icon.svg`, and inline in each page's `.brand` lockup). Replace it with the designer's SVG when it arrives; search for `M5.2 60.4`. 83 - **Where green and lime appear, and nowhere else:** the icon (lime mark on green: favicon and the pictured notifications), one "working" dot in the hero, and selected text. Do not add bands, panels, buttons or headings in them. 84 - The download and getting-started pages show the apps' own icons (`img/icon-app.png`, `img/icon-host.png`), copied from the asset catalogs in `ripul-native-app`. Copy them again whenever the app icons change, so the site shows what people will see in their Dock. 85 86 ## Deploy 87 88 ```bash 89 cd website 90 npx wrangler deploy 91 ``` 92 93 It is a Cloudflare Worker called `ripul-site` that serves `public/` as static assets, on the Ripul account, answering on the route `app.ripul.io/*` (`wrangler.jsonc`). It does not go through `deploy:all` or Trainyard. Check it with `curl -sI https://app.ripul.io`. 94 95 It is a route rather than a custom domain because `app.ripul.io` still has its old proxied DNS record, which pointed at the retired splash server, and the wrangler login cannot edit DNS. The route answers in front of that record, so the old server is never reached. Do not delete the record without replacing it: the route needs a proxied record to exist. To tidy up, delete it in the Cloudflare dashboard and switch the route to `{ "pattern": "app.ripul.io", "custom_domain": true }` in the same sitting. 96 97 ## Who it is for 98 99 Developers first (Peter, 9 October 2026): they are the app's primary audience, and the goal is that using Ripul's tools makes them want the SDK in their own apps. The SDK is part of the main story, not a footnote: it has a section on the home page, a place in the menu ("For developers") and its own page (`/features/sdk/`). When writing about a tool, it is fair to say that the reader's own app can have it too. The look and the plain wording stay as they are; developers read plain English as well. 100 101 ## Local models 102 103 Added 9 October 2026 at Peter's request: a feature page (`/features/local-models/`), a row on the home page under "Independent by design", and a help guide (`/help/local-models/`). What they say comes from the Mac host (`ripul-native-app/macOS/LocalModelCatalog.swift`, the Local Models block of `CliSettingsScreen.swift`) and the web app (`chrome-extension/src/shared/localModelCatalog.ts`). Only LM Studio has been tried, so the pages name no other server. 104 105 **Local models and Direct are two halves of one promise** (Peter, 9 October 2026). Direct answers how the phone reaches the Mac (nothing through Ripul); a local model answers who does the thinking (nothing to an AI company); both together mean only your own machines are involved. It is told as three settings, chosen per conversation, and it lives on the privacy page (`/features/privacy/`, "All the way"), with a panel on the home page and a pointer from the local models page. It is the far end of the dial, not the headline: signing in stays the way in. Peter is proving the claim himself with the internet off; if that finds an exception, add it to "What still reaches outside" on the privacy page. 106 107 Left out on purpose, until it has shipped in both the web app and the Mac host: choosing how many tools each model is given (Everything, No Ripul tools, Lean, Chat only) and saving a model under a name of your own (`chrome-extension/src/shared/personalModels.ts`). It deserves a section on the feature page when it is live. 108 109 ## Writing for it 110 111 - The reader may never have opened a terminal. Say what they get, in everyday words. No code, no command lines, no developer icons, no dark "hacker" screens. 112 - The pictures of the app are drawn in HTML (`.phone`, `.sheet`, `.notes`) so they can show plain-language conversations. Use a real screenshot only when it looks like something a customer would recognise. 113 - British spelling. No exclamation marks, no "simply", no "just". 114 - Every claim has to be true of the shipped app. The in-app guides (`chrome-extension/src/logging/react-sidepanel/pages/help/helpContent.ts`) are the source for what the app does; this site retells them for a wider audience and does not replace them. 115 - The story page is the founder's own words. Keep the specifics. 116 - **Installing: lead with the one-line Terminal install** as the fastest and easiest way; the disk images are the alternative (Peter, 8 October 2026). 117 - **Connecting: signing in to both devices is the way in.** Direct pairing is for people with a confidentiality concern; mention it as an option for them, not as a setup step, and do not recommend it otherwise (Peter, 8 October 2026). 118

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__browser_list_targets
entries.description: Discover browsers, their handles, capabilities and current availability, and this session's selected browser. Browser tab IDs belong to one browser; list tabs again after switching targets.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__browser_open_tab
entries.description: Open a URL in a new browser tab on this device and wait for it to load. Bare hosts are fine — "itv.com" is upgraded to "https://itv.com". active.description: Make this the browser's current tab. Defaults to true. It does not put the tab in front of the person.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__presentImages
entries.description:
Show the user images inline in the chat — a screenshot or picture you
have as a file on the host, a link, or base64 — so they can see what you
see without opening a file.

**When to use:** whenever the user should see an image you have but no
tool result already shows it: a screenshot you saved to disk
(e.g. `ripul-bridge screenshot ... shot.jpg`), an image you generated or
downloaded, a picture at a URL. Images that a tool already returned (a
bridge screenshot, a screen frame) are shown automatically — do not
present those again.

**Sources (one per image):**
- `path` — a file on the Mac host (absolute, `~/...`, or relative to the
  session's working directory). Any format macOS can read, including
  HEIC; large images are downscaled.
- `url` — an http(s) link to an image.
- `base64` — raw base64 or a `data:image/...;base64,` URL.

Up to 4 images per call. You also receive each image back, so you can
check what was shown. Refer to the images in prose ("the screenshot
above") instead of repeating paths.

images.description: The images to show, in display order.

base64.description: Base64 image bytes, or a data:image/...;base64, URL.

mediaType.description: MIME type for base64 when it cannot be detected — image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp or image/gif.

name.description: Optional file name shown when the user enlarges or saves the image.

path.description: Image file on the Mac host — absolute, ~/..., or relative to the working directory.

title.description: Optional short label for what the images show.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__ripul_guide
entries.description:
How to use Ripul, the harness this conversation runs in, one topic at a time. Read the relevant guide BEFORE the work it covers: Ripul has its own way of doing several things an agent would otherwise do with a built-in feature.

Call with no arguments for the current list of guides and when to read each. Call with `topic` to read one. Topics include:
- `session`: what ends your process, long-running jobs, what a commit does, asking the user, spoken messages. Read once at the start of work.
- `artefacts`: the user asks for an artefact or anything interactive. Make it a Ripul artefact, not an artifact or canvas of your own.
- `trains`: before you build, deploy, install to a phone or simulator, or test against something another agent may be using.
- `devices`: putting a build on an iPhone, or looking at, tapping through or recording an app on a phone, tablet or simulator.
- `browser`: a page your own fetch cannot read, or one that needs the user's sign-in; before any browser_ tool.
- `plans`: the user asks for a plan or design document, or for a review of one. Write a Ripul plan, not a plan in your own plan mode.
- `voice-and-media`: a message wrapped in <voice>, or an image, video, recording or files to show in the chat.
- `cms`: building or changing a site, portal or dashboard in the Ripul CMS.
- `sdk`: the repository is an iOS app that uses, or should use, the RipulAgent package.

topic.description: The id of the guide to read, for example `artefacts`. Leave out to list the guides.

content.text:
{"guide":"# The browser tools

Ripul has a real browser that you can drive: `browser_open_tab`, `browser_read_page`, `browser_run_js`, `browser_list_tabs`, `browser_close_tab`, `browser_hand_over` to show a tab to the person, and `browser_list_targets` to choose which browser. This guide applies when you need a web page as a browser sees it.

## When to use them, and when your own fetch is enough

Use your own web fetch or search first for ordinary pages. It is quicker, it touches nothing the user can see, and it leaves no tabs behind.

Use the browser tools when:

- **The page is built by JavaScript.** A fetch reads the HTML the server sent, so a client-rendered page comes back as a title, a shell or "no results". If a fetch returns far less than the page obviously holds, open it in the browser before concluding anything about the page.
- **The page needs a sign-in.** Tabs you open share cookies and storage with the tabs the user opens in the same Ripul browser, so a site they signed in to there is signed in for you. Sign-ins from Safari or Chrome are not there. If the site is not signed in, ask the user to sign in in Ripul's browser; do not ask for a password.
- **You need to act on the page or measure it**: click, fill in a form, read computed values.
- **The page is on the Mac itself.** The Mac's browser can reach `localhost` on the Mac; a phone's browser cannot, because `localhost` there is the phone.

## Targets

A target is one browser. Every `browser_…` tool takes an optional `target`, and `browser_list_targets` lists the ones this chat knows, with each handle, whether it is reachable now, and which one is selected.

- `background` is the browser inside Ripul Host on the Mac. It is there whenever the host is, whichever device the user is on. It has a desktop-sized page (1280 wide). It is missing from the list when the user has switched on Hide Host Tools.
- A handle such as `iphone-c603` is the browser inside the Ripul app on that phone or tablet. It is not Safari. It has a phone-sized page and a mobile user agent, so sites serve their mobile layout.
- A handle starting `web-` is a desktop browser that has Ripul open with the Ripul browser extension installed. Its tabs are the user's own tabs, with their own sign-ins.

Choose by what the task needs: `background` for research and for anything that should keep working when the user walks away; a phone when the question is how the page behaves on a phone.

## How the selection behaves

The chat has one selected browser. A call with no `target` uses it. Before anything is selected, the first call uses the browser on the device where the chat started, if that device has one, and otherwise `background`.

- **Passing `target` changes the selection** for every later call, not only that one. After one call to a phone, name `background` again to go back.
- **The selection does not follow the user.** If the conversation moves from the Mac to a phone, calls keep going to the browser you were using, because that is where your tabs are. `here` means the browser where the chat started, not the device the user holds now. Switch only when the user names a device.
- **An unreachable browser is an error**, never a quiet switch to another one. Call `browser_list_targets` and choose again.
- **Tab ids belong to one browser** and start again when its app restarts. Call `browser_list_tabs` after switching target and before reusing an old id.
- Every result carries `_target`, `_targetReason` (`explicit`, `pinned` or `default`) and `_device`. When a call moved the selection, `_selectionChangedFrom` names the browser it left. Read them: an empty tab list from the wrong browser looks the same as "no tabs open".

## Whose browser it is, and when the owner is asked

Every browser you can reach belongs to the chat's owner. `background` is the one inside Ripul Host, and it is yours to use in the owner's own turns. Every other target is one of the owner's own browsers, with their tabs and their sign-ins, and needs their say first.

- **The first call to one of those asks the owner.** A card appears in the chat ("Allow in this chat", "Allow once", "Don't allow") and your call comes back refused: nothing ran. Say in the chat what you want to do there and why, then stop. Call again only after the owner has answered.
- **`browser_list_tabs` still answers before that**, with ids and load state only. Titles and addresses are hidden until the owner allows the browser.
- **`browser_list_targets` shows `access` for each target**: `open`, `allowed by the owner`, `waiting for the owner's answer` or `needs the owner's approval`.
- **A refusal is final for that browser for now.** Do not try another of the owner's browsers to get round it, and do not look through their tabs for one that happens to be signed in.

### Chats with invited people

A chat can hold its owner and people the owner invited. In a turn an invited member asked for, the browser is **theirs**, not the owner's.

- **A call with no `target` runs in the member's own browser**, the one inside their Ripul app, signed in as them. The result says so: `_target` is their `member-…` handle, `_targetReason` is `requester`, and `_notice` names them.
- **They must be sharing it.** Sharing is the member's own choice, made on their own device, for one chat. If they are not sharing, the call is refused, a card in the chat asks them, and nothing runs anywhere: it never falls back to a browser of the owner's. Say what you need the browser for, stop, and call again after they have shared it.
- **Only the `browser_…` operations reach a member's browser**, and only in a turn that member asked for. In the owner's turns, and in another member's, it is refused.
- **The owner's browsers are closed in a member's turn, `background` included**, because the host's browser may hold the owner's sign-in, with rights far wider than the member's. Naming one as `target` asks the owner ("Allow for one hour", "Allow once", "Don't allow", per browser and per member). Only the owner's answer counts. Do this only when the work truly needs the owner's rights, and say so in the chat first.

`browser_list_targets` returns `requestedBy`, a `note`, and the member's browser as a target when they are sharing it. When the owner has allowed one of theirs, do only what the member asked and say in the chat what you did there.

## The person cannot see a tab you open

A tab you open is made off screen. It loads and you can read and script it, but the person whose browser it is sees nothing, and cannot click in it. Results say so:

- `visibleToPerson` is on every tab, and on what `browser_read_page` and `browser_run_js` return. `false` means nobody is looking at that page. `active` only means "the browser's current tab": the browser itself may be closed.
- `width` and `height` are what the page is really laid out at. On a Mac that is a desktop size (1280 wide), on an iPhone a phone size. Pass `viewport: "desktop"` (or a width from 768 to 3840) to `browser_open_tab` for a desktop layout anywhere.
- In the Ripul apps a small picture of the tab you are using appears over the chat. It is a picture: it takes no clicks. Its Open button takes the person to the real page.

So never ask someone to click or type in a tab while `visibleToPerson` is false. Hand it over first.

### Handing a tab to the person

`browser_hand_over` puts the tab in front of the person: their Browser comes forward on that tab, your `message` sits above the page, and there is a Done button. Use it whenever a step is theirs to do: a sign-in, a passkey or code, a captcha, a choice only they can make. Never ask for a password in the chat, and never type one for them.

- `message` is one plain sentence saying what to do: "Sign in to business.wac.rocks, then tap Done."
- It waits, and returns `finished`: `done` (they tapped Done), `url-changed` (the page settled on another address, usually the sign-in completing), `closed`, or `still-waiting` after about 40 seconds. On `still-waiting`, call it again with the same tab to keep waiting; say in the chat what you are waiting for.
- After `done` or `url-changed`, read the page before going on: check that it is where you expect.
- `wait: false` shows the tab and returns at once, for "have a look at what I did".
- It needs a browser with a screen: a Ripul app on a phone or a Mac. The host's `background` browser has no screen and refuses; open the page in the person's own browser instead. A desktop browser reached through the extension does not offer it yet.
- If the result has `visibleToPerson: false`, their app is closed or in the background. Ask them in the chat to open Ripul.

## Reading a page, or running script in it

`browser_read_page` returns the page's visible text, everything in it, menus and footers included, cut at 8000 characters unless you raise `maxChars`. `truncated` says whether it was cut. Use it to read an article or documentation page.

Use `browser_run_js` when you want one part of a long page, structured data, an attribute, or to click or type. Write an expression whose value is the answer, such as `[...document.querySelectorAll('h2')].map(h => h.innerText)`. Return strings, numbers, arrays and plain objects. Do not count on a promise being awaited: start the work, store the result on `window`, and read it with a second call.

## Things that go wrong

- **Read too early.** `browser_open_tab` waits for the page's load event, not for the script that fills it in. If the text is thin, poll with `browser_run_js` for the element you expect, then read.
- **Dialogs.** A page that calls `alert`, `confirm` or `prompt` puts a real dialog on the user's screen and your call waits for someone to answer it. Do not trigger one.
- **Taking over the user's view.** `browser_open_tab` makes the new tab the active one unless you pass `active: false`. With no `id`, read and run act on the active tab, which may be the user's. Pass the `id` you were given.
- **Leftover tabs.** Close every tab you opened. Do not close tabs you did not open.
- **Logs.** `host_console_logs` and `host_network_logs` report the Ripul Host app itself, not pages in browser tabs. To see what a page logged or requested, collect it inside the page with `browser_run_js` (for example `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')`).

- It waits, and returns `finished`: `done` (they tapped Done), `url-changed` (the page settled on another address, usually the sign-in completing), `closed`, or `still-waiting` after about 40 seconds. On `still-waiting`, call it again with the same tab to keep waiting; say in the chat what you are waiting for.
- After `done` or `url-changed`, read the page before going on: check that it is where you expect.
- `wait: false` shows the tab and returns at once, for "have a look at what I did".
- It needs a browser with a screen: a Ripul app on a phone or a Mac. The host's `background` browser has no screen and refuses; open the page in the person's own browser instead. A desktop browser reached through the extension does not offer it yet.
- If the result has `visibleToPerson: false`, their app is closed or in the background. Ask them in the chat to open Ripul.

## Reading a page, or running script in it

`browser_read_page` returns the page's visible text, everything in it, menus and footers included, cut at 8000 characters unless you raise `maxChars`. `truncated` says whether it was cut. Use it to read an article or documentation page.

Use `browser_run_js` when you want one part of a long page, structured data, an attribute, or to click or type. Write an expression whose value is the answer, such as `[...document.querySelectorAll('h2')].map(h => h.innerText)`. Return strings, numbers, arrays and plain objects. Do not count on a promise being awaited: start the work, store the result on `window`, and read it with a second call.

## Things that go wrong

- **Read too early.** `browser_open_tab` waits for the page's load event, not for the script that fills it in. If the text is thin, poll with `browser_run_js` for the element you expect, then read.
- **Dialogs.** A page that calls `alert`, `confirm` or `prompt` puts a real dialog on the user's screen and your call waits for someone to answer it. Do not trigger one.
- **Taking over the user's view.** `browser_open_tab` makes the new tab the active one unless you pass `active: false`. With no `id`, read and run act on the active tab, which may be the user's. Pass the `id` you were given.
- **Leftover tabs.** Close every tab you opened. Do not close tabs you did not open.
- **Logs.** `host_console_logs` and `host_network_logs` report the Ripul Host app itself, not pages in browser tabs. To see what a page logged or requested, collect it inside the page with `browser_run_js` (for example `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')`).

content.content:
---
name: Do not screen-grab to verify, ask Peter
description: Simulator screenshots burn tokens for a weak signal; build, deploy, then ask Peter to test and report
metadata:
  type: feedback
  scope: person
---

September 21, 2026: Peter asked me to stop taking simulator screen grabs to verify changes, and to ask him to test instead.

**Why:** a screenshot costs a large image in context for a weak signal, and it tells you less than Peter looking at the device does. During the browser toolbar work I burned several on the Duo and the iPhone sim, and the one reading that mattered — the address field vanishing rather than shrinking to a pill — came from Peter's eye, not from my captures. He had also already said he would test and report back, and I ran the test anyway.

**Simulators too.** On September 21 he added: test on his physical iPhone, not on simulators — "we don't need to do 400 simulator builds, I can test it for you on the iPhone". Build and install to the device (`xcrun devicectl device install app`) and let him drive. The simulator had also been throwing WebKit JIT crashes that were not reproducible on device, so sim results were costing time and telling us nothing.

**How to apply:** build, install to his iPhone, then stop and ask him to test, naming exactly what to look for and on which device. Use `xcrun simctl io ... screenshot` only if he asks for one. Instrumented measurements that return text — XCUITest frames, `app.debugDescription`, log greps — are still fine and are the right tool when a number settles the question. Same spirit as [[feedback_user_tests_microphone]].
----
c425e93b5 2026-10-09 New chat: an empty chat takes its look from the website
In Ripul's own apps an empty chat now opens with the cut-dot mark and a small label for what the chat talks to, a serif heading with its last words in italic, and plain rows divided by hairlines with a dot of colour each instead of an icon chip. The accents are the website's teal, coral, gold and lilac, lightened for dark. Site-key customers keep their own themed screen; what a tap does is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__browser_close_tab
entries.description: Close a browser tab on this device by id.

id.description: Tab id to close, as reported by browser_list_tabs.

target.description: Browser handle returned by browser_list_targets, or background for the session host browser. Omit to use this session's selected browser. The initial selection uses the session origin when known. here refers to the session origin browser. An explicit target changes the selection. Selection survives disconnects and reloads; an unavailable selection fails without switching browsers. In a turn an invited member asked for, omit target to use that member's own browser. Any browser of the chat owner's other than background, and every one in a member's turn, needs the owner's approval first: the call is refused and the owner is asked. Check _target and _device on the result.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_inspect_screen
entries.description: Inspect the running app's on-screen native (UIKit/SwiftUI) view tree. Returns elements with class name, role (button/field/cell/list/... — the vocabulary the actuation tools' role predicate matches), window-space frame, accessibility id / uiKitIdentifier stamp, visible text, owning view controller, and IBOutlet/property name — for locating a control in source. Every element also gets a short-lived "handle" (e.g. "e7") — pass it to tap_element / type_text / scroll_element to hit exactly that element. Handles go stale on the next inspect or actuation. Set includeScreenshot for a downscaled JPEG. Excludes the Ripul dev-assistant overlay itself, so it reports the host app's screen, never the assistant. Only what can be seen is returned: views scrolled or clipped out of sight, and interactive views covered by something else (a closed sidebar under the main screen), are left out and counted in `hidden`; includeHidden returns them too, marked. Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

filter.description: Only include elements whose class, text, id, IBOutlet or view controller contains this substring (case-insensitive)

includeHidden.description: Also return views that can't be seen (covered, clipped or off screen), each marked with `hidden`

includeScreenshot.description: Also return a base64 JPEG of the screen (downscaled)

maxElements.description: Cap the number of elements returned (default 250, max 1000)

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_list_targets
entries.description: Discover known remote devices: their handles, models (e.g. "iPhone 16 Pro Max"), current availability, tool capabilities, and which agent holds each one. Also shows this chat's working device. Use a handle as the device argument of a device tool. Availability is checked again when the tool executes.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_screen_frame
entries.description: One frame of the host app's screen for a live view: a JPEG (base64) and the window size in points, the space touch uses. Pass since=<the previous frame's id>: if the screen hasn't changed the result is unchanged:true with no image. Excludes the Ripul dev-assistant overlay. Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

maxDimension.description: Long side of the image in pixels (240–1200, default 640)

purpose.description: "liveview" when a Live View viewer asks; leave out otherwise

since.description: The previous frame's id; an unchanged screen then returns no image

viewer.description: The Live View viewer's name, shown on this device while it watches

content.text:
The new-chat screen is the only place in the app where the brand appears, so it reads as a website page dropped into an app that is otherwise stock iOS and Material. You're right that it doesn't align.

I measured the website live; the app-side values are from code. I could not look at the new-chat screen rendered, because the simulator was showing another session's Intent Lab and I left your phone alone.

| Surface | Text face | Display face | Accent | Canvas (light / dark) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Website | Archivo | Instrument Serif | teal `#1f6f70`, navy buttons | paper `#f8f4ec` / navy `#1b1d2e` |
| App icon | none | serif wordmark | lime mark | navy |
| Native screens | SF Pro | SF Pro bold | system blue (`AccentColor` is empty) | system grey and white / black |
| Chat web view | Roboto labels, SF message text, Segoe UI/Roboto tool calls | none | blue `#0078d4` | white / `#000` |
| New-chat screen | Roboto | Instrument Serif | website teal, plus coral, gold and lilac dots | white / `#000` |

On that one screen you get three typefaces, two accents (teal on the screen, blue in the composer and header around it), and the site's warm colours on a pure black or white canvas.

My recommendations, in the order I would do them:

1. **One accent: the website teal.** Set `AccentColor` and the first-party web theme's primary to `#1f6f70` light / `#62b9b4` dark. Fold in the three other teals already in the chat: user messages (`#00897B`), tool calls (`#4a90a4`) and the secondary (`#40e0d0`). Gate it on the first-party presentation so site-key customers keep their themes.
2. **One text face in the app: the system font.** Point the first-party web theme at the system stack and drop Roboto and the Segoe UI tool-call font. I would not bring Archivo in; it would make the same seam against the native screens.
3. **Make the serif the app's display face, or remove it.** I would keep it, since the icon already carries it. Bundle Instrument Serif natively and use it for onboarding titles, What's New, pricing and empty states, never for navigation titles, rows or buttons.
4. **Quieten the new-chat screen.** Use one teal dot instead of four colours, because colour in the app already means provider, chat and status. Bring the heading down from 40 to about 34 on the phone, to sit on the iOS large-title scale.
5. **Leave the canvas neutral.** Paper brought in one screen at a time recreates this problem; it is a whole-app decision for later. The Help sheet is then the one cream surface, and could take the app's canvas when shown in the sheet.
6. **Redraw the website's phones afterwards.** They show navy bubbles on paper, which the real app does not have.

Items 1 and 2 are web changes plus one colour set, which needs a native rebuild. Item 3 needs an SDK helper and builds of both apps.

I changed nothing. The tree has uncommitted work from another session (three modified files, two untracked), which I left alone.

Say go and I'll start with 1 and 2.

Load this when a user asks to add Turnstile, set up CAPTCHA, protect a form or endpoint from bots, or fix a Turnstile integration. Mirrors developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/spin.
- web-perf: Analyzes web performance using Chrome DevTools MCP. Measures Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) and supplementary metrics (FCP, TBT, Speed Index), identifies render-blocking resources, network dependency chains, layout shifts, caching issues, and accessibility gaps. Use when asked to audit, profile, debug, or optimize page load performance, Lighthouse scores, or site speed. Biases towards retrieval from current documentation over pre-trained knowledge.
- workers-best-practices: Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- wrangler: Cloudflare Workers CLI for deploying, developing, and managing Workers, KV, R2, D1, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Workers AI, Containers, Queues, Workflows, Pipelines, and Secrets Store. Load before running wrangler commands to ensure correct syntax and best practices. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:google-workspace: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

# Claude

## Project Overview

Ripul is an AI-powered workflow automation platform. This is the monorepo containing all three packages.

### Monorepo Structure

```
ripul/
├── chrome-extension/     Web application + lightweight Chrome extension
├── ripul-native-app/     SwiftUI app (iOS + macOS) wrapping the web app
├── ripul-ios-sdk/        Swift Package bridging native apps ↔ web agent
└── website/              Public site at app.ripul.io (plain HTML, own deploy — see website/README.md)
```

| Package | Tech | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| **chrome-extension** | React 19, TypeScript, Cloudflare Pages/Workers | Primary codebase — web app deployed to `demo.ripul.io` (the canonical app host; all clients load it from there), plus a minimal Chrome extension for browser API proxying |
| **ripul-native-app** | SwiftUI, iOS + macOS | Native shell wrapping the web app in WKWebView with native tools, push notifications, Live Activities, CLI servers (macOS) |
| **ripul-ios-sdk** | Swift Package | Core bridge library — AgentView, AgentBridge, NativeTool protocol, capability system, web↔native communication |

### How They Fit Together

```
chrome-extension (web app)
        │ Embedded in WKWebView via agent-framework:* message protocol
ripul-native-app (native shell)
        │ imports RipulAgent SPM package
ripul-ios-sdk (bridge library)
```

The web app auto-detects its runtime context:
- **web-only** — standalone browser, graceful fallback
- **bridged** — minimal Chrome extension present
- **native** — running in WKWebView with native capabilities

### Development Focus
- **DO**: Develop features in the web application (chrome-extension)
- **DO**: Keep the lightweight Chrome extension minimal (only browser API features)
- **DON'T**: Frame this project as "a Chrome extension" — it's a web application
- **DON'T**: Add new features to the legacy full extension code

---

## Documentation

Each package has its own docs. Key cross-cutting references:

| Document | Location | Contents |
|----------|----------|----------|
| **PROJECT-STRUCTURE.md** | `chrome-extension/docs/` | Cross-repo architecture, message protocol, build commands |
| **GLOSSARY.md** | `chrome-extension/` | Core domain terms (Tool, Prompt, PromptTool, MCP, etc.) |
| **NATIVE-BRIDGE-ARCHITECTURE.md** | `chrome-extension/docs/` | Native iOS ↔ web communication patterns |
| **iOS Styling Guide** | `ripul-native-app/docs/` | Native glass effects, vibrancy, glass modifier library |
| **Build & Deploy** | `ripul-native-app/docs/` | How to build, install, and run on macOS and iOS |
| **[Tools System Architecture](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/toolsSystemArchitecture.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | End-to-end guide: definitions → interceptors → handlers → CLI bridge → native tools |
| **[Private functions and store builds](ripul-native-app/docs/app-store-private-apis.md)** | `ripul-native-app/docs/` | What is private, which builds may carry it, the check that stops an upload, the pre-submission checklist |
| **[MCP Tool Surfaces](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/mcpToolSurfaces.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | Cross-package map of every MCP/tool surface: why each context exists, consumers, transports, prefixes (`host_`/`device_`/`web_tool_`), gates. Start here for anything spanning CLI/native/device/extension tools |
| **[The Ripul Library](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/artefactLibrary.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | The public library of artefacts: the rules (one revision, reviewed before it is listed, copy, report, block), storage, routes, where it shows on the web, in the apps and to agents, and the tests |
| **[Ripul guides](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/ripulGuide.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | How product knowledge reaches agents on other people's repos: the one-paragraph harness note, the `ripul_guide` tool, and the guides in `public/guides/`. How to add a guide |
| **[The command orchestrator](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/commandOrchestrator.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | A fast hosted model (Haiku) that turns one spoken sentence into app actions, with the app's registered actions as its tools. How to switch it on, how a request flows, the rules it keeps, what was measured, limits and tests |
| **[Shell chats](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/shellChats.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | The Shell model: a chat whose messages run as commands in a zsh on the Mac host. What it does, its limits, how a turn flows, the server routes, the files and the tests |
| **[Workflow runs](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/workflowRuns.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | How a Claude Code workflow run shows its phases and agents in a chat: what the CLI sends, the record a finished run leaves, the limits, and what is not built (stopping a run) |
| **[Sub-agents in a chat](chrome-extension/docs/architecture/agentRuns.md)** | `chrome-extension/docs/architecture/` | How a sub-agent shows as a full-width row in a chat, the row a workflow run has: what the CLI sends for it, where its title, totals and latest actions come from, the limits, and what is not built |

---

## Common Commands

### chrome-extension (Web App)

> **No local dev server.** The workflow is: edit → TypeScript check → `deploy:all`. All clients (browser, iOS, macOS) load the web app from Cloudflare. Do not start or look for a local dev server.

> **Deploys go through Trainyard.** `npm run deploy:all` boards the web train rather than deploying. It needs a pushed commit on `main`, and it waits and then reports what went live. One run serves every agent waiting. It holds while anyone is testing, refuses to ship a held-back commit, and reloads the host only when the other agents are idle. **Before a test that depends on the live build or the host, take a hold**: `ripul-train hold host-webview --reason "…" --ttl 20`, then `ripul-train release <id>` when done. For "don't ship this yet", use `ripul-train block <commit> --reason "…"`. Check the state with `ripul-train status`. Rebuild the Mac host with `ripul-train request mac-host --wait`, not a raw `xcodebuild`, so the relaunch waits for every agent's turn to end. iPhone, simulator and TestFlight builds board trains too: `ship_ios.py` / `ship-ota.sh`, `ship_duo_sim.py` and `deploy-testflight.sh` request the `ios`, `ios-sim` and `testflight` tracks by themselves, and all native tracks share one lane, so builds queue instead of failing on the release lock. They ship committed work only. Take `ripul-train hold iphone` while testing on the phone. `deploy:all:direct` skips all of this; `deploy:all` falls back to it by itself if Trainyard isn't running. Details are in `ripul-native-app/macOS/trainyard/README.md`, and the design in `docs/plans/agent-build-trains.md`.
>
> **Concurrent deploys queue; they no longer corrupt each other.** `build:prod` starts with `clean` (`premove public/js`), and wrangler uploads by listing `public/` then opening each file — so a build started by *any* session used to delete the files another session's upload was midway through sending. Symptom: `Failed to upload files … ENOENT: chunk-<build>-<hash>.js`, or an upload that crawls (459s measured, against 13s uncontended). `deploy:pages` now runs under a machine-wide lock (`scripts/with-deploy-lock.mjs`, atomic mkdir on `/tmp` — macOS has no `flock`). A second deploy waits and says who it is waiting for; a dead holder is detected by PID and its lock broken.
>
> **A healthy `deploy:all` is ~35 seconds.** If one runs into minutes, suspect contention rather than bandwidth.
>
> **Never trust the deploy exit code alone.** Wrangler can crash *inside its own error handler* (`TypeError: The "code" argument must be of type number. Received type string ('ENOENT')`) and still exit 0, and `concurrently` then runs the `&& seed` chain on top of a Pages deploy that never happened — so a failed deploy prints success end to end. `deploy:all` now ends with `verify:pages`, which compares the built `public/version.json` against the live `demo.ripul.io/version.json` (with no-cache headers — the custom domain can serve a stale `version.json` even past a query-string buster) and fails loudly on a mismatch.

```bash
cd chrome-extension
npm run build            # esbuild → public/js/
npm run build:prod       # Production build with minification
npm run build:extension  # Minimal extension → dist/minimal-extension/
npm run deploy:all       # Board the web train: pages + worker + webhook + seed tools + verify
npm run deploy:all -- --checked   # …when you already ran tsgo on this exact commit
npx tsgo --noEmit        # TypeScript check (required after changes)
```

### ripul-native-app

See [Build & Deploy docs](ripul-native-app/docs/build-and-deploy.md) for full details including OTA/IPA deployment.

```bash
cd ripul-native-app
xcodegen generate           # Required after clone or project.yml changes

# iOS — build and install to device (requires USB or same Wi-Fi)
# Use -derivedDataPath build so both steps read/write the same pinned location.
# Without it, ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/RipulNativeApp-*/ may match
# stale dirs from old checkouts and you'll install a stale binary.
xcodebuild -scheme RipulApp \
  -destination 'platform=iOS,id=00008150-001C544E0EBA401C' \
  -derivedDataPath build \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=C7AA358R56 CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic \
  build
xcrun devicectl device install app \
  --device 00008150-001C544E0EBA401C \
  build/Build/Products/Debug-iphoneos/Ripul.app

# iOS — OTA deploy (when device is not on the network)
# ship-ota.sh uses -configuration Debug (same as device builds) and the shared
# ripul-native-app/build DerivedData — so .o files are reused across device
# builds, OTA archives, and the Alice variant. First run ~3-5 min, warm ~30 sec.
# NEVER write ad-hoc scripts — fresh /tmp/ paths + Release config = full cold build.
nohup bash ripul-native-app/scripts/ship-ota.sh > /tmp/ship-ota.log 2>&1 & disown
# Skip Alice: SKIP_ALICE=1 nohup bash ripul-native-app/scripts/ship-ota.sh ...
# Progress: tail -f /tmp/ship-ota.log

# iOS — TestFlight (the front door for testers who are NOT on the device list)
# Dev OTA embeds a UDID list, so a new tester costs a UDID + registration +
# rebuild. TestFlight costs an email. Use it for anyone outside your inner loop;
# keep ship-ota.sh for your own iteration. ~15-20 min. Full runbook:
# ripul-native-app/docs/testflight-deploy.md
nohup bash ripul-native-app/scripts/deploy-testflight.sh > /tmp/ripul-testflight.log 2>&1 & disown
# Archive + export without uploading anything to Apple: ... deploy-testflight.sh export
# This is the ONE sanctioned exception to the "no fresh /tmp + Release" rule
# above: App Store signing REQUIRES Release, and a Release archive shares no .o
# files with the Debug caches, so it must not be pointed at build/.

# macOS — NOTE the separate DerivedData (`build-mac`, not `build`).
# `build` is the SHARED iOS DerivedData (device builds, ship-ota.sh's SHARED_DD,
# the Alice variant). A fresh build into it recreates Build/Products, which
# DELETES the macOS Debug/Ripul.app sitting there — and because the Dock
# bookmarks that bundle by path, the Ripul icon turns into a question mark and
# the host won't launch (observed 2026-09-07). Keeping macOS in its own
# DerivedData makes it immune to any iOS build. Dock THIS path.
xcodebuild -scheme RipulMac -destination 'platform=macOS' -derivedDataPath build-mac \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=C7AA358R56 CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic build
open ripul-native-app/build-mac/Build/Products/Debug/Ripul.app
```

### iPhones away from the Mac — `ripul-bridge` (Tailscale)

Agents: use the `host_bridge_*` tools (`bridge_status`, `bridge_install`, `bridge_ship`, `bridge_screenshot`, `bridge_debug`, …) — the Mac host wraps the command for you; people use **Devices** in the iPhone or Catalyst sidebar (one list of phones, with Live View of their apps and, under Whole Screen, the [device runner](ripul-native-app/device-runner/README.md) for everything else on the phone), and Settings → iPhones over Tailscale on the Mac to set up. A phone pairs by being plugged into the Mac once: nothing to choose or press (`ripul-bridge autopair`, run by the host when a phone is plugged in). Underneath, `ripul-native-app/device-bridge/ripul-bridge` does Xcode-level work on a paired iPhone anywhere on the tailnet: `install` (exact build read back), `launch`, `terminate`, `screenshot`, `debug` (attached LLDB), `mount-ddi`. `ship-ios.sh` uses it automatically when CoreDevice can't see the phone (route order CoreDevice → bridge → OTA; `--transport bridge` forces it). Start with `ripul-bridge status --deep`. The phone must be on **Wi-Fi or another phone's hotspot** with Tailscale on; on its own cellular it refuses new tunnels. `debug` remounts the disk image itself after a phone reboot; `ripul-bridge symbols <phone>` fetches debug symbols over the network once per iOS version. ### DerivedData: the sanctioned paths, and no others

These are the only sanctioned `-derivedDataPath` values. Use one of them. Never invent a new one.

| Path | Used for |
|---|---|
| `ripul-native-app/build` | iOS **device** + simulator-less archives, and `ship-ota.sh` (its `SHARED_DD`) |
| `ripul-native-app/build-variant-alice` | the Alice variant (`ship_ios.py` drives this; do not reuse it for anything else) |
| `ripul-native-app/build-iossim` | **iOS Simulator**, including iPhone Duo (`ship_duo_sim.py`) |
| `ripul-native-app/build-mac` | native macOS (`RipulMac`) |
| `ripul-native-app/build-mac-alice` | Ripul Host Alice, the second host for clean installs (`build_mac.py --variant alice`) |
| `ripul-native-app/build-catalyst` | Mac Catalyst (`RipulApp`, `variant=Mac Catalyst`) |

They are separate *on purpose*, for two different reasons.

**Products would delete each other.** An iOS build into `build` recreates `Build/Products`, which deletes a macOS or Catalyst `Ripul.app` sitting at the same path — that is what turns a Docked icon into a question mark.

**One Xcode: 27.1.** Every script builds with `/Applications/Xcode-27.1.app`, on both Macs, and no other Xcode should be installed beside it (Peter, 5 October 2026: "we need to be on 27.1 and that's it"). To try a newer one, use `ripul-native-app/scripts/try-xcode.sh`, and remove the old one when moving over. Before that date the two Macs held seven copies of four versions and scripts preferred different ones: the same commit was built with different toolchains on each Mac, and two toolchains sharing one DerivedData cost a full cold rebuild on every alternation. That is where the separate `build-iossim` came from. It stays: the scripts and their warm caches are built around these paths.

**Why this rule exists.** Sessions kept inventing a fresh path for one-off builds — `build-sim`, `build-simulator`, `build-iossim-artefacts` were three more names for the same simulator job — and nothing ever deleted them. By 2026-09-15 there were 16 such directories holding **26.4 GB**, and 18 `Ripul.app` bundles claiming the same two bundle ids. A throwaway path also costs you a *cold* build every time, since it shares no `.o` files with the warm caches. Those duplicates were deleted on 2026-09-25; `build-iossim` is the one simulator path that survives. Do not recreate the others.

If you genuinely need an isolated build, put it under `/tmp` so it cannot accumulate, and say so in your report.

### Which Ripul am I running?

Two different apps ship from this repo. They are separate applications, not two builds of one:

| App | Scheme | Bundle id | Display name | Icon |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mac host | `RipulMac` | `io.ripul.mac` | **Ripul Host** | teal |
| Catalyst | `RipulApp` | `io.ripul.app` | **Ripul** | navy |

Both produce a bundle named `Ripul.app` and both can sit in the Dock at once — hence the distinct display names and icons. Do not "fix" either back to a shared name or icon; that is the whole point of them.

To see what is actually running, by path:

```bash
pgrep -lf "Ripul.app/Contents/MacOS/Ripul"
```

Launch by **path**, never by bundle id. `open -b io.ripul.mac` can resolve to a stale copy — e.g. a months-old `/Applications/Ripul.app` — rather than the build you just made.

**One host per checkout, enforced.** A Debug Ripul Host that is not this checkout's `build-mac` product opens the canonical one and exits (`macOS/CanonicalHostGuard.swift`). Set `RIPUL_ALLOW_NONCANONICAL_HOST=1` to run a deliberate test copy. **And one running host per profile, enforced.** The host and its watchdog each hold a kernel lock in the profile's Application Support folder (`macOS/SingleInstanceLock.swift`, `SingleHostGuard.swift`); a second launch of the same profile brings the first forward and exits, and a second watchdog exits. Before 8 October 2026 two watchdogs could watch one host, and each reopened it when it exited. A host that keeps its own folder, installation id and login runs beside the real one: that is what a variant such as Alice is, so test a second instance with a variant. The one sanctioned second host is **Ripul Host Alice** (`io.ripul.mac.alice`): a different bundle id, so the guard leaves it alone. `python3 ripul-native-app/scripts/build_mac.py --variant alice --fresh` wipes it back to a first install and launches it beside the real host ([build-and-deploy.md](ripul-native-app/docs/build-and-deploy.md#a-second-host-for-clean-installs-ripul-host-alice)). Both run as `…/Ripul.app/Contents/MacOS/Ripul`, so stop hosts by full path, never `killall Ripul`. `build_mac.py` also unregisters every other `io.ripul.mac` copy from LaunchServices after each build. **One running Catalyst app per install, too.** A second copy of `io.ripul.app` (an installed one beside a developer build, or `open -n`) brings the first forward and closes within about three seconds (`iOS/SingleRunningCopy.swift`). Two copies share one installation id and fight over one relay seat; on 2026-10-07 that sent a phone 12-38 MB a minute. So to run a new build, quit the running one first. `RIPUL_ALLOW_SECOND_COPY=1` lets a deliberate second copy run.

Never copy the host into `/Applications` or keep backup `.app`s beside the product: on 2026-09-26 a March build in `/Applications` had been hosting for five days and answering the phone.

## Private Apple functions never ship in a store build

Ripul is going to the App Store. App Store review rejects private Apple functions, so a build that reaches **TestFlight or the App Store must contain none**. Development builds may: Live View's real touches are private, and are compiled into Debug builds only.

1. **Compile it out, don't switch it off.** Any line that reaches a private function (by `dlsym`, a selector or class name built from a string, an underscore key, an underscore override) goes inside `#if DEBUG || RIPUL_DEVELOPER_BUILD`. A runtime check leaves the name in the binary.
2. **Never set `RIPUL_DEVELOPER_BUILD`, and never use a Debug configuration, for a build going to TestFlight or the App Store.** Never put either in a project file, xcconfig or scheme. `RIPUL_DEVELOPER_BUILD` belongs only on the command line of a direct install to your own device.
3. **Run the check; don't trust memory.**
   ```bash
   python3 ripul-native-app/scripts/check_private_apis.py source          # the code
   python3 ripul-native-app/scripts/check_private_apis.py all <app|ipa>   # the code and a built app
   ```
   `deploy-testflight.sh` runs it on the app it is about to upload and refuses when it fails. A developer-only name in the app, or a lookup nobody has reviewed, has no override.
4. **`RIPUL_ALLOW_KNOWN_PRIVATE_APIS=1` is for tester builds only**, while the known uses remain. **Never for a build submitted for App Store review.**
5. **Ripul Host (the Mac host) is distributed directly, not through the Mac App Store.** It uses private macOS functions to give windows keyboard focus.

Known uses still in every build on 29 September 2026: the in-app browser's mouse (`iOS/BrowserNativeMouse.swift`, the real risk), agent actuation of alerts and recognizers, the keyboard bar subclass, and a demangler lookup. The inventory, the ways out and the pre-submission checklist: [app-store-private-apis.md](ripul-native-app/docs/app-store-private-apis.md).

## Proving the build is live (do this FIRST — never unravel bundles)

When something looks broken on a client (Mac/iOS/web), **do not theorize about stale builds or pull apart chunks.** There is one immediate signal:

1. **Deployed version (server):** `curl -s https://demo.ripul.io/version.json` → `{ "version": "...", "builtAt": "..." }`. (`demo.ripul.io` is the canonical app host — all clients, including the native iOS/macOS shells, load it from there. Static file, served by Pages, not `/api`.) NOTE: `app.ripul.io` is **not the app** — since 8 October 2026 it is the public website (`website/`, a separate Cloudflare Worker), so it has no `version.json`, `/popup` or `/js/*`. Do not use it to check builds or assume the app is hosted there.
2. **Running version (client):** the app logs at boot, via `console.log`:
   - `[RIPUL] build=<version> origin=<host>`
   - `[RIPUL] LIVE ✓ running=<v> deployed=<v>` **or** `[RIPUL] STALE ✗ running=<v> deployed=<v>` (it self-checks against `/version.json`).

`LIVE ✓` (or running == deployed) → on the current build, **move on; not stale.** `STALE ✗` → force a reload/relaunch. (Wiping web data is NOT a staleness test — login persists via a native-injected session; trust the version signal.) `version.json` is written by `scripts/build.mjs` and matches `__BUILD_VERSION__` in the bundle.

`chrome-extension/public/version.json` is **gitignored, not tracked** — it is regenerated on every build, and `deploy:pages` rebuilds it immediately before upload, so the deployed file never comes from git. Never commit it, never `git add` it, and never treat its absence from `git status` (or its on-disk contents) as a problem.
