tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_open_app_url
entries.description: Open one of this app's own deep links in the running app (e.g. ripul://open-chat?id=<chat id> to open a chat, ripul://agents for the Agents list). Only the app's own URL schemes are accepted. Deterministic navigation for on-device tests; follow with wait_for_element or inspect_screen to confirm where it landed. Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

url.description: A URL in one of this app's own schemes

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_set_working_device
entries.description: Move this chat to another device, or hand its device back. The working device is where every device_* tool acts when a call names no device. Moving takes the device for this chat alone (other agents' device calls to it are refused) and hands the previous one back. Use it only when the user asks to move; a message from another phone does not move the chat. Pass `release: true` when the work on the device is done, so other agents can use it.

device.description: The device to move to: a handle from device_list_targets (e.g. "iphone-c603") or a model name that matches one device (e.g. "iPhone 16 Pro Max").

release.description: Hand the device back instead of moving. The chat then has no working device.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_tap_element
entries.description: Tap an on-screen element (button, row, tab) in the host app. Addressing is a predicate query — every given predicate ANDs together, XPath-style: handle (preferred, exact) > id/text/role/class, optionally scoped by 'within'. Example: within={text:"Alice"}, role="button" taps the button inside Alice's row. Ambiguous queries (several disjoint matches) FAIL with a candidate list — refine with within/role/id, or pass nth. Nested duplicates (button + its label) collapse to the container, except that a SwiftUI element's own stamp beats a larger container that adopted its id. A handle stays valid after other taps while its element hasn't moved or changed. text also presses a system alert's button (e.g. text="Cancel"). Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

handle.description: Handle from the last inspect_screen (e.g. "e7") — taps exactly that element (preferred)

id.description: Accessibility id / uiKitIdentifier of the element (exact)

nth.description: 0-based ordinal when several disjoint elements match (last resort)

touch.description: Press it with a real finger touch at its centre instead of its control or accessibility action (debug builds). Used automatically when nothing else can press the element.

within.description: Anchor container: search only inside its subtree, e.g. {text:"Alice"} for the row containing Alice

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_touch
entries.description: Real finger input in the host app at a point in window coordinates (points — the space inspect_screen's frames use): tap, double_tap, long_press, swipe from x,y to toX,toY, or pinch about x,y with two fingers going from `from` to `to` points apart (apart to zoom in). It goes through UIKit's own touch handling, so gesture recognizers, SwiftUI, tab bars and scroll views react as to a finger. Use it for gestures (swipe to scroll, drag, long press), for an exact spot, or where tap_element reports an element isn't tappable. A short swipe duration flings, a long one drags. The result names what was under the finger; confirm the effect with wait_for_element or inspect_screen. Debug builds of the app only. Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

angle.description: pinch: the line the fingers are on, in degrees from the horizontal (default 45)

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

duration.description: Seconds: long_press hold (default 0.8), swipe or pinch travel (default 0.25)

from.description: pinch: how far apart the two fingers start, in points (default 80)

purpose.description: "liveview" when a Live View viewer sends it; leave out otherwise

to.description: pinch: how far apart they end, in points (default 240)

toX.description: swipe: where the finger lifts, x

toY.description: swipe: where the finger lifts, y

x.description: Where the finger lands: x in window points

y.description: Where the finger lands: y in window points

content.text:
No, I'd leave the typeface alone in both the session list and the sidebar. They should stay on the system font, and looking at them on the sim, they already do the right thing.

- **The rows need weights the serif doesn't have.** An unread chat is shown by a bold title, and Instrument Serif ships in regular and italic only. It is also a display face, and the detail line under each title is 12pt.
- **They sit among system controls.** The search field, the filter menu, the New Chat buttons and swipe actions are all the system font, so any other face in the rows makes a seam on every line.
- **They scale with the user's text size.** Titles are `.body`, details `.caption`, times `.caption2`, so they follow Dynamic Type without extra work.
- **The sidebar already carries the brand.** The serif wordmark with the lime dot sits at the top (`SidebarView.swift:80`). One wordmark above plain system rows is the right amount.

That last point corrects what I said before: the new-chat screen is not the only branded place in the app. The wordmark is also in the sidebar and on the loading screens. So the gap is narrower than I made it sound: the serif is used for the logo and one heading, and nothing in between.

Three small things I would change in the list, none of them the typeface:

1. **The tool label under a row's icon is fixed at 8pt** (`UnifiedSessionRow.swift:397`). That is too small to read and ignores text size. I'd raise it to `.caption2` or drop it and let the subtitle carry the tool name. This is from code; no row was running a tool when I looked.
2. **Section headers could match the website's eyebrow.** MACHINES and SESSIONS are already uppercase, semibold and grey (`GlassComponents.swift:67`). Adding the eyebrow's letter-spacing, and using the same style for the small label on the new-chat screen, would tie the list to that screen without changing the font.
3. **The model name is the loudest text in each row.** "Opus 5.5" is orange beside an orange icon on every line. That is colour, not font, and it looks deliberate, so I'd only revisit it when the accent moves to teal.

On the sim I closed the Intent Lab sheet another session had open, opened and closed the sidebar, then handed the sim back. That sheet looked in use, since its sentence had changed between my two looks, so whoever was running it will need to reopen it. No code changed.

Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is October 2026 — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__device_speak
entries.description:
Speak text aloud to the user in a hands-free voice conversation.

A user message wrapped in <voice>...</voice> markup was spoken aloud — the user is listening, not reading. When the latest user message carries this markup, talk to them through this tool and close your turn by speaking the answer. The markup applies per message: a later user message WITHOUT it means the user is back to typing and reading, so reply in writing and stop speaking.

Write for the ear: one to three short conversational sentences, plain prose only — no markdown, no code, no tables, no file paths, no URLs, no identifiers. When your reply contains that kind of material, refer the listener to the screen instead (for example, "the diff is in the chat").

You may call this several times in one turn: a brief acknowledgement when you start, an occasional plain-language progress note during long work, and a closing call that delivers the answer. If you speak at all during a turn, finish by speaking the answer — your written reply is not read aloud when you have spoken for yourself.

Returns spoken=false when no voice conversation is active. That means nobody heard it: stop calling this for the rest of the turn and put your answer in the written reply as normal. Runs on a remote device. Call device_list_targets to discover devices and their capabilities; pass device to select one.

device.description: Optional. Target a specific connected REMOTE device by its handle (e.g. "iphone-c603") — the value returned as `_device` on a previous result, and the only form guaranteed unique. A display name also works when it matches exactly one device; if it matches several the call fails and lists the handles. If omitted, this chat's working device is used (see device_list_targets); a chat without one uses the only connected device, and several connected devices fail. A device another agent holds refuses the call.

I've completed the web search for Claude iOS app typography fonts. Here are the key findings:

## Typography Fonts Used

Claude.ai uses **Anthropic Sans** for body and navigation at 17px / 400 weight, while the hero headline switches to **Anthropic Serif** at 56px / 330 weight.

## Font Stack Details

The display font stack includes "Anthropic Serif", "Tiempos Headline", Georgia, and other serif fallbacks, while the body uses "Anthropic Sans", "Söhne", system-ui, and other sans-serif fallbacks.

## Design Approach

Styrene by Berton Hasebe is applied to website headlines and subheadings, while Tiempos by Klim Type Foundry is used for body text. 

The Claude chat interface renders user messages and AI replies in different fonts—their serif is a variation of Tiempos by Klim Type Foundry, and the sans appears to be Styrene, designed by Berton Hasebe.

## Design Philosophy

Anthropic is trying to distance themselves from a technological visual style and seeking to make designs of their products friendlier, with chat appearing visually similar to any other messenger chat.

content.text:
Yes, I overstated it. "Use the system font" is a safe default, not a rule, and Claude is a good counterexample. (Speaking didn't go through, as no voice conversation was active, so this is written.)

**What Claude does:** it ships two brand typefaces and uses them throughout. A serif sets Claude's replies and the headings; a sans sets your own messages, the sidebar and the controls. These were Tiempos and Styrene, and are now Anthropic Serif and Anthropic Sans. The sources I found describe the web app. I believe the iPhone app follows the same split, but I couldn't inspect it from here.

**What that changes for Ripul:**

- **Archivo could be the app's text face.** It is a variable font with every weight, so bold-for-unread works, and custom fonts can still follow the user's text size. This reverses my earlier "don't bring Archivo in".
- **The serif still stays out of rows.** Claude's serif is a text face built for long reading. Instrument Serif is a display face with one weight, so it keeps to headings and the wordmark.

**The cost:**

- **Chat:** the web chat is one theme change and a deploy.
- **Native:** there are about 2,080 font settings across the app and SDK. System-drawn parts such as navigation titles, the search field, menus and alerts stay in the system font unless styled separately.

**What I'd do:** trial Archivo on the session list and sidebar only, plus the chat. Those two native surfaces run through three shared components, so it is a small change. You look at it on your phone, then decide whether the rest is worth it. One thing to check in the trial is whether Archivo has fixed-width digits, since row timers rely on them.

Say go and I'll build the trial.

Sources:
- [Styrene in use: Anthropic (type.today)](https://type.today/en/journal/anthropic)
- [Claude design summary (webdesignhot)](https://www.webdesignhot.com/design.md/claude-ai/)

=== project_theme_framework_sdk_lift.md
---
name: theme-framework-sdk-lift
description: "Phased lift of WAC's theme framework into the RipulAgent SDK — phase 1 (mechanism) DONE at SDK 0.5.7; vocabulary stays host-owned; phase 2 = generic-over-vocabulary engine"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 26dfe389-0b13-448a-8746-15ba840f778e
  modified: 2026-07-26T13:38:01.067Z
  scope: repo
  repo: ripul
  scope_also: repo:wac-ios
---

WAC's theme framework is being lifted into the RipulAgent SDK in phases (user direction,
2026-07-26). Decomposition: **mechanism** (generic, SDK-worthy) vs **vocabulary** (token
enums, palette, Theme.json, scopes, component-shaped knob sets — always host-owned) vs
**surfaces** (Theme Editor, pickers — later).

**Phase 1 — DONE (SDK `259d32900`, public v0.5.7; WAC `a355e9c19`, OTA 202607261058):**
- `ThemeInstrumentation.swift` (SDK): `UIColor.ripulToken`/`ripulTagged`/`ripulAlpha`,
  `UIView.ripulBackgroundToken` + setter swizzle + `RipulThemeInstrumentation.install()`,
  `Notification.Name.ripulThemeDidChange`, `refreshesOnThemeChange()` (read-the-state fix +
  placement rule), `ripulThemedHostingController(rootView:)` → `UIHostingController<AnyView>`.
- `ThemeRemap.swift` (SDK): `RipulThemeRemapOptionRow`/`RipulThemeRemapSection`/
  `RipulThemeRemapTarget` protocol, `RipulThemeRemapSheetPresenter` (`onLog` host hook) +
  `RipulThemeRemapSheetView` (system-styled). The sheet is now the explorer's built-in
  double-tap UX for ANY host that vends targets.
- WAC migration: symbols renamed (wacToken→ripulToken etc., whole-tree sed); WAC's
  `.themeDidChange` ALIASES `.ripulThemeDidChange` (one notification drives both);

content.text:
Yes, that's right, and cobbler's children is fair. The SDK has a full theming system and WAC is built on it, but Ripul's own app doesn't use it at all. (Speaking didn't go through again, so this is written.)

| | WAC app | Ripul app |
|---|---|---|
| Registers a theme with the SDK engine | Yes | No, only a fixture for UI tests (`RipulAppApp.swift:289`) |
| Theme document | 30 colours, 37 semantic labels, 25 component tokens, 18 metrics, a font family | None |
| Code reading theme tokens | 47 files, about 220 places | None |
| Served from Ripul's backend, editable in the app, review and publish | Yes | No |
| Accent colour | A token | An empty colour asset, so system blue, used directly in about 140 places |
| Fonts | One setting re-fonts the app | About 2,080 direct system-font calls |

The session list and the other screens the SDK itself provides read no tokens either. So Ripul ships the theme editor inside an app that has no theme.

Two gaps in the SDK matter for the font question:

- **Fonts are not in the engine.** It handles colours and style settings. WAC's font family lives in WAC's own part of its theme document, read by WAC's own code.
- **The engine is UIKit-first.** WAC is mostly UIKit and Ripul is SwiftUI. I found a refresh modifier and a themed text view for SwiftUI, but no colour or font token a SwiftUI view can simply read.

So I'd change my proposal: do the session list and sidebar trial on tokens instead of hard-coding Archivo.

1. Add font tokens and SwiftUI colour and font accessors to the SDK. WAC could later move its font setting onto the same mechanism.
2. Give Ripul a small theme of its own: the website's palette, an accent, and a type scale.
3. Move the session row, the section headers and the sidebar rows onto it first, then the rest screen by screen.

Each font and colour call still has to be touched once, the same work as the hard-coded trial. After that, system font versus Archivo, and blue versus teal, are settings you can flip from the theme editor on your phone rather than something we argue in advance.

The web chat has its own separate theme system, so it would need the same values passed to it or set to match.

Say go and I'll start with step 1 and the session list.

content.text:
{"guide":"# Plans

In Ripul a plan is a design document in the repository that can be reviewed: people and agents file comments against its sections, the author answers them, and the fixes become tasks. The user reads and acts on plans in the **Plans** screen of the Ripul apps, where each plan shows as Open or Locked with its comments and tasks. Use this guide when asked to write, review, revise or carry out a plan.

## What a plan is made of

A plan is three files that share a name in `docs/plans/` of the chat's working directory:

- `<slug>.md` is the plan itself, in prose. This is the only file you write by hand, with your normal file tools.
- `<slug>.plan.jsonl` is the log of comments, replies, status changes and tasks. Only the plan tools add to it.
- `<slug>.review.md` is a readable review, rebuilt from the log on every change. Never edit it.

No tool creates a plan. To start one, write `docs/plans/<slug>.md` with a title and `##` sections (the Plans screen starts new plans with Problem, Approach and Open questions). If a file with that name already exists, it is someone's plan: revise it or choose another name.

These are ordinary repository files. The plan tools write to the working directory without asking the user for approval, and they do not commit; commit the files with the rest of your work.

## Which to use: a Ripul plan, or your own plan mode or todo list

When the user asks for a plan, a design or a proposal they will read or have reviewed, write a Ripul plan. Your built-in plan mode and todo list live inside your own session: the user cannot open them in the Plans screen, another agent cannot comment on them, and nothing records what was agreed. Keep your own todo list for private working steps. Work the user should see as owed on a plan goes in with `planTask`.

Plans are not artefacts: the artefact tools do not read or write them. If the user wants a visual summary of a plan, build that separately (see the `artefacts` guide) and keep the Markdown file as the source.

## The tools

| Tool | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `planStatus` | Read a plan's state: section anchors, outstanding comments, open tasks, Open or Locked. Call it first, every time. |
| `planComment` | File a review comment against a section. |
| `planReply` | Discuss a comment without changing its status. |
| `planResolve` | Move a comment to `accepted`, `resolved` or `wontfix`. |
| `planTask` | Record work owed, usually linked to an accepted comment. |
| `planTaskStatus` | Move a task between `open`, `doing`, `done` and `dropped`. |

Each acts on the plan in the working directory of the chat you are running in.

## Statuses and what moves them

**Comments** go one way: `open` to `accepted`, `resolved` or `wontfix`, and `accepted` to `resolved` or `wontfix`. `resolved` and `wontfix` are final and the tool refuses to move a comment back. This stops a later round reopening what an earlier one settled. If there is something new, file a new comment.

**Locked is computed, not set.** A plan is Locked when no `blocking` comment is `open` or `accepted`. You cannot mark a plan done; you can only clear what holds it open. `accepted` still holds it open: agreeing a fix is needed is not confirming it was made.

**Tasks** move freely in both directions. Take them one at a time: `doing` when you start, `done` when the work is finished. Marking a task `done` does not close the comment it came from; the reviewer does that.

**Severity** matters: `blocking` holds the plan open, `should-fix` is a real gap that does not, `nit` is editorial. Use `blocking` only for what would be expensive to find out later.

## Reviewing a plan

1. `planStatus`, to get the anchor list. An anchor is a section's heading turned into a slug. A shortened slug works if it matches exactly one section; an anchor that matches none, or more than one, is refused. Use `__plan__` for a remark about the plan as a whole.
2. `planComment` for each finding, with the defect, why it matters and a proposed fix.
3. On a later round, first check each `accepted` comment against the revised text. Mark it `resolved` if the change answers it; if not, `planReply` and leave it. Then review the plan again for anything new.

## Answering a reviewer's comment

1. `planStatus`, which lists outstanding comments with the hardest first.
2. Where you agree, edit the plan file to fix it, then `planResolve` with `accepted`, and `planTask` with `fromComment` for any work that remains.
3. Where you disagree, `planResolve` with `wontfix` and your reason in `note`. A decline without a reason will be raised again. Use `planReply` to argue the point or ask a question.
4. Do not mark someone else's comment `resolved`. That is the reviewer's confirmation that the fix is real. Sessions started from the Plans screen to draft or address a plan are refused it on comments they did not file. You may resolve a comment you filed yourself.

## Things that go wrong

- **Renaming or removing a heading orphans its comments.** They are kept and listed by `planStatus` as orphaned. When revising, keep existing headings and add subsections instead.
- **`planStatus` lists at most 40 anchors, comments and tasks each**, with long comment bodies cut short and no replies. For the full text and the replies, read `<slug>.review.md`.

4. Do not mark someone else's comment `resolved`. That is the reviewer's confirmation that the fix is real. Sessions started from the Plans screen to draft or address a plan are refused it on comments they did not file. You may resolve a comment you filed yourself.

## Things that go wrong

- **Renaming or removing a heading orphans its comments.** They are kept and listed by `planStatus` as orphaned. When revising, keep existing headings and add subsections instead.
- **`planStatus` lists at most 40 anchors, comments and tasks each**, with long comment bodies cut short and no replies. For the full text and the replies, read `<slug>.review.md`.

== theming guide head
# Theming Guide

How to use the theme system correctly in React components.

## Architecture

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/themes/index.ts` | Exports 7 theme variants + helper functions |
| `src/themes/ThemeProvider.tsx` | `AppThemeProvider` context — manages mode, persistence, custom themes |
| `src/themes/types.ts` | TypeScript extensions for MUI theme (custom palette + section configs) |
| `src/shared/mui/useThemeColors.ts` | `useThemeColors()` hook — memoized, pre-calculated theme-aware colors |

## Available Themes

| Mode | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `darkGradient` | Default. Purple/blue gradient aesthetic |
| `darkFlat` | Clean dark without gradients |
| `darkMinimal` | Minimal dark |
| `darkGlass` | Glass morphism effects |
| `darkNeon` | Bright neon accents |
| `darkAurora` | Aurora borealis palette |
| `light` | Light mode (Windows Fluent Design colors) |

Theme is persisted in storage via `appThemeMode` key. Custom AI-generated themes override the selected mode.

## How to Use Colors in Components

### Preferred: MUI sx prop tokens (string shorthand)

MUI resolves dot-notation strings against the theme palette automatically in `sx` props. This is the simplest and most common pattern.

```tsx
<Box sx={{
  color: 'text.primary',
  bgcolor: 'background.paper',
  borderColor: 'divider',
}} />

<Typography sx={{ color: 'success.main' }} />

<Box sx={{
  bgcolor: 'action.hover',        // subtle background for hover states
  '&:hover': { bgcolor: 'action.selected' },  // slightly stronger on hover

== first-party presentation
import type { SiteKeyFeatures } from '../types/siteKey';

/** Presentation only: these profiles never grant tools, accounts or models. */
export type ChatPresentation = Pick<SiteKeyFeatures,
  'uiScale' | 'inlineThinkingFontSize' | 'inlineThinkingMaxHeight' | 'chatBottomBuffer'
  | 'hideWelcomeScreen' | 'welcomePromptStyle' | 'welcomePromptSource'
  | 'showAgentAvatar' | 'agentAvatarIcon' | 'hideGutterOnMobile'
  | 'toolCallFontFamily' | 'toolCallIcon' | 'toolCallSummaryLayout' | 'toolCallSummaryMode'
  | 'mastheadGlassStyle' | 'chatInputLayout'>;

// The first-party iPhone appearance, adopted from its published view context
// (bookmarklet-copy-copy-2, 2026-09-14). Normal and Standalone import this same
// definition. Change presentation here for both; site-key permissions remain
// independently resolved. Per-chat tool expansion preferences stay untouched.
export const RIPUL_IPHONE_PRESENTATION: Readonly<ChatPresentation> = Object.freeze({
  uiScale: 1.15,
  inlineThinkingFontSize: 1.15,
  inlineThinkingMaxHeight: 0,
  chatBottomBuffer: 93,
  // An empty chat opens with a few rows for what it talks to (config/chatStarters.ts).
  hideWelcomeScreen: false,
  welcomePromptStyle: 'compact',
  welcomePromptSource: 'chatKind',
  showAgentAvatar: false,
  agentAvatarIcon: '',
  hideGutterOnMobile: true,
  toolCallFontFamily: "'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif",
  toolCallIcon: 'robot',
  toolCallSummaryLayout: 'chips',
  toolCallSummaryMode: 'list',
  mastheadGlassStyle: 'clear',
  chatInputLayout: 'twoRow',
});

/** An explicit native app opt-in; other SDK apps and portals keep their context. */
export function chatPresentationFromURL(href: string): Readonly<ChatPresentation> | undefined {
  const url = new URL(href);
  const hash = new URLSearchParams(url.hash.slice(url.hash.indexOf('?') + 1));
  if (hash.get('native') !== 'true') return undefined;
  return hash.get('chatPresentation') === 'ripul-iphone' ? RIPUL_IPHONE_PRESENTATION : undefined;

entries.description:
Read the review state of a plan: its addressable anchors, what is still
outstanding, open tasks, and whether it is locked.

**Call this before commenting on a plan.** Comments anchor to section
slugs, and a reviewer that has not seen the anchor list will invent
slugs that resolve to nothing.

A plan is three files sharing a slug in docs/plans/ — `<slug>.md` (the
prose), `<slug>.plan.jsonl` (the append-only comment and task log), and
`<slug>.review.md` (rendered from the log). Only the body is written by
hand; the other two are maintained by these tools.

"Locked" means no blocking comment is outstanding. It is computed, not
declared — you cannot mark a plan done, you can only resolve the
comments that are holding it open.

input.content:
# A theme-aware codebase

**Status**: draft for review, 10 October 2026. Nothing is built.
**Depends on**: the SDK theme engine (shipped, SDK 0.5.10 onward), `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/remote-themes.md`
**Reference host**: `WAC_ios_final` (branch `v3`), the one app built on the engine today

## Problem

Ripul's website has a brand: a warm paper canvas, navy ink, a teal accent, Archivo for text and Instrument Serif for headings. Ripul's apps do not carry it. The native screens are stock iOS (system font, system blue), the chat is Material (Roboto, blue `#0078d4`), and the one branded screen, the empty chat, sits between them looking like a page from the website.

The cause is not taste, it is plumbing. The SDK has a theme engine, a hosted theme document, an in-app theme editor and a review-and-publish flow. WAC is built on all of it. Ripul's own app uses none of it: every font and colour is written at the call site, so "use teal" or "try Archivo" means editing thousands of lines, and nobody can try a look on a phone before deciding.

This plan makes every colour and typeface in the first-party apps come from a theme, without changing how anything looks. A second, small step then applies the brand as a theme document that can be switched on a phone.

## What exists today

Measured on `main`, 10 October 2026.

| Surface | State |
|---|---|
| SDK theme engine | 19 files, about 6,100 lines: three tiers of colour tokens, named styles, remote document with cache and bundle fallback, editor, review and publish, View Explorer readout, label and tab-title text overrides |
| WAC | Registers a vocabulary (`WACThemeSpec.make()`), 47 files and about 220 call sites read tokens, theme document served from `llm-proxy.ripul.io/v1/app-themes/wac-v1` |
| Ripul app | Configures the engine only in a UI-test fixture (`iOS/RipulAppApp.swift:289`). `AccentColor` is an empty asset, so the accent is system blue |
| SDK's own screens | Read no tokens. One file checks whether a theme exists (`Sessions/RipulSolutionsScreen.swift:389`) |
| Web chat | Seven MUI themes and a theming guide, but the themes set no font family (so Roboto), and `src` holds about 2,060 hex literals, 2,000 `rgba(` literals and 790 `fontFamily` values outside the theme files |
| Website | The palette and the two faces as CSS variables in `website/public/css/site.css` |

Native call sites that set a font or a colour directly:

| Directory | Files | Fonts | Named colours | Accent or tint | `.primary`/`.secondary` | System backgrounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ripul-native-app/iOS` | 131 | 556 | 143 | 83 | 374 | 84 |
| `ripul-native-app/Shared` | 86 | 133 | 23 | 9 | 128 | 3 |
| `ripul-native-app/macOS` | 125 | 204 | 30 | 18 | 143 | 11 |
| `ripul-ios-sdk/Sources/RipulAgent` (all) | 447 | 1,366 | 268 | 186 | 1,042 | 138 |

Of the font calls in the iPhone app and SDK, about 1,530 use a text style (`.body`, `.caption`) and about 400 use a fixed size. The first kind can be rewritten by a script. The second kind, the named colours and the backgrounds need a decision each: about 1,100 sites.

### Three gaps in the engine

The engine was lifted from WAC, and WAC is a light-only UIKit app.

1. **No fonts.** The engine resolves colours and style knobs. WAC keeps its font family in its own part of the document and reads it with its own helper (`Font.theme`, `UIFont.themeFontName`).
2. **One value per colour.** A primitive is a single hex. There is no light and dark pair and no way to name a system colour. WAC sets `UIUserInterfaceStyle` to `Light`. Ripul follows the system appearance.
3. **UIKit only.** `ThemeEngine.swift` is inside `#if os(iOS)` and returns `UIColor`. SwiftUI gets a refresh modifier and a themed text view, but no colour or font a view can read. The SDK also builds for macOS 14, where none of this compiles.

A fourth point is structural: the engine holds one vocabulary per process, the host's. The SDK's screens are shown inside WAC as well as inside Ripul, so they cannot read tokens that only Ripul's app registers.

## Decisions

### 1. The first theme is today's look, exactly

The default values of every token are what the code does now: the system font at the system sizes, the system accent, the system backgrounds. A migrated call site therefore renders the same pixels as before. This is what lets many agents land small commits on `main` in any order, and it gives one acceptance test for the whole migration: nothing changed.

It needs two things from the engine. A colour must be able to name a system colour (`system:label`, `system:systemBackground`, `system:tint`) and resolve to the live dynamic colour, so light, dark and increased contrast stay exact. A type role whose family is `system` must return the system text style itself (`Font.body`), not a custom font that resembles it.

### 2. The brand is a second document, applied last

Teal, Archivo and the serif arrive as a theme document after the migration is done, switchable from the theme editor on a phone. The questions argued in the chat that led to this plan (system font or Archivo, blue or teal, neutral canvas or paper) become settings to look at, not decisions to make first.

### 3. A small vocabulary, named for the job

Tokens are named for what they are for, never for their value. The list is in "The vocabulary" below. A leaf agent that needs a token the list lacks does not invent one: it asks the foundation owner, who adds it or names the existing one.

### 4. The SDK owns a base vocabulary beside the host's

The SDK registers its own tokens under a reserved `ripul.` prefix, with defaults in code that give the system look. They resolve in any host, with or without a host theme. Ripul's app supplies a document that overrides them. WAC's vocabulary and document are untouched, and its `Theme.json` stays valid byte for byte.

### 5. Shared places before call sites

A root modifier, the sheet wrapper (`ripulSheet`), the hosting controllers (24 of them), the glass helpers and the shared row components are fixed first. If SwiftUI carries a root foreground style and tint down to `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tint` and `Color.accentColor`, about 1,700 call sites need no edit at all. The foundation proves or disproves that with tests before any leaf work starts (see F3).

### 6. One document for native and web

The chat is a web view inside the native app, so the two must agree. The theme is one JSON document in the repository. The native app bundles it and the web build reads the same file to make the first-party MUI theme. Site-key customers keep their own themes: the first-party theme applies only under the first-party presentation (`config/chatPresentation.ts`).

### 7. A check whose count only falls

A script counts direct fonts and colours per file and compares with a committed baseline. A count above the baseline fails the build. Agents lower the baseline as they migrate. This stops the tree refilling behind them, and its total is the progress measure. `scripts/check_sheet_sizing.py` is the model: it already runs as a pre-build step.

### 8. What is exempt

Some colours and sizes are not theme. They stay, marked with `// theme-exempt: <reason>` so the check can count them apart:

- SF Symbol sizes. A font on an `Image` is an icon size, not type.
- Colours that are data: a provider's or model's colour, a chat's colour, terminal ANSI colours, syntax and diff colours.
- Brand marks: the Claude and Codex marks, the wordmark's lime dot.
- System materials and glass.
- Views that exist only in `#if DEBUG` harnesses.
- Customer content: `CmsRender/` in the SDK and `src/cms` on the web follow the customer's portal theme (`CmsPortalTheme`), not Ripul's.

## The vocabulary

Proposed. F1 fixes the final names in `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/theming.md`, and that file is what leaf agents read.

Colour roles, each with a light and a dark value:

| Role | Default (today's look) | For |
|---|---|---|
| `accent` | `system:tint` | Selection, links, primary buttons, the unread mark |
| `onAccent` | white | Text and icons on an accent fill |
| `canvas` | `system:systemBackground` | The app's background |
| `surface` | `system:secondarySystemGroupedBackground` | Cards and grouped rows |
| `surfaceSunken` | `system:systemGroupedBackground` | The ground behind cards |
| `text` | `system:label` | Primary text |
| `textSecondary` | `system:secondaryLabel` | Detail lines |
| `textTertiary` | `system:tertiaryLabel` | Timestamps, hints |
| `separator` | `system:separator` | Hairlines |
| `success` | `system:systemGreen` | Online, done |
| `warning` | `system:systemOrange` | Waiting, caution |
| `danger` | `system:systemRed` | Errors, destructive actions |

Type roles. Each has a family, a size, a weight, the text style it scales with, and tracking:

| Role | Default |
|---|---|
| `largeTitle`, `title`, `title2`, `title3`, `headline`, `body`, `callout`, `subheadline`, `footnote`, `caption`, `caption2` | The system text style of the same name |
| `display` | `title` in the system font. The brand theme makes it the serif |
| `eyebrow` | `subheadline`, semibold, uppercase: today's section header |
| `code` | The system monospaced face |

Three families are named in the document: `text`, `display` and `code`. A role may carry a second size for Mac Catalyst, which has no Dynamic Type and where the sidebar already uses fixed 14 and 12 point text (`SidebarRowMetrics`).

Corner radii and spacing are not in this plan (see Open questions).

## Foundation

These land before any leaf work. F1 to F5 are one agent's work in the SDK and app. W1 is a second agent's work on the web. The two do not share files.

**F1. Engine.** Light and dark pairs and `system:` references for colours. Font tokens: families, roles, Dynamic Type. The resolution core compiles on macOS; only the repaint walker and UIKit tagging stay behind `#if os(iOS)`. The base vocabulary of decision 4. All additive: an existing document with hex-only colours and no fonts must load unchanged, and the seven existing theme test files must pass.

**F2. Accessors.** What a view writes. Proposed: `Color.ripul(.accent)`, `Font.ripul(.body)`, `Font.ripul(.caption, weight: .semibold)`, `Font.ripul(size: 14, weight: .medium)` for a fixed size in the theme's family, an icon-size helper for symbols, and UIKit equivalents. A unit test asserts that with the default document each accessor equals the system value it replaces (`Font.ripul(.body) == Font.body`). That test is the proof of decision 1.

**F3. Roots.** A `ripulThemeRoot()` modifier that sets tint, foreground style and default font and refreshes on theme change, applied at both `WindowGroup`s, inside `ripulSheet`, and in the hosting controllers. Tests that answer, for a window, a sheet, a popover and a hosting controller: do `.secondary`, `.tint` and `Color.accentColor` follow the root? The answers go in `theming.md` as the rule leaf agents follow. Where the answer is no, those call sites join the leaf work.

**F4. Ripul's document.** One JSON file at a path both builds can read, registered by the app at launch. With the default values it is nearly empty. The Solutions screen then shows the theme editor for Ripul's own theme.

**F5. The check and the rewrite script.** `ripul-native-app/scripts/check_theme_tokens.py` with its baseline, wired into the pre-build steps beside the sheet check. A rewrite script for the mechanical cases (`.font(.body)` and its `.weight`, `.bold()`, `.monospacedDigit()` forms), which leaf agents run on their own files.

**F6. Reference screens.** A script that puts the simulator into a fixed state (launch arguments and fixture data, as the UI tests do), captures about a dozen screens in light and dark, and reports a pixel difference per screen as text. Run once before leaf work to make the baseline.

**W1. Web foundation.**
- Give the theme a `text`, `display` and `code` family and move the first-party font choices into it (today: Roboto by default, `'Segoe UI', Roboto` for tool calls in `chatPresentation.ts`, the serif inside `V2StarterScreen.tsx`).
- Generate the first-party light and dark MUI themes from the shared document, with today's values as the default.

2. Foundation: F1 to F6 and W1, two agents in parallel.
3. S1 alone, to shake out the accessors.
4. The remaining streams in parallel: up to eight native and three web.

- Every reference screen is unchanged with the default document, in light and dark.

# A theme-aware codebase

**Status**: draft for review, 10 October 2026. Nothing is built.
**Depends on**: the SDK theme engine (shipped, SDK 0.5.10 onward), `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/remote-themes.md`
**Reference host**: `WAC_ios_final` (branch `v3`), the one app built on the engine today

## Problem

Ripul's website has a brand: a warm paper canvas, navy ink, a teal accent, Archivo for text and Instrument Serif for headings. Ripul's apps do not carry it. The native screens are stock iOS (system font, system blue), the chat is Material (Roboto, blue `#0078d4`), and the one branded screen, the empty chat, sits between them looking like a page from the website.

The cause is not taste, it is plumbing. The SDK has a theme engine, a hosted theme document, an in-app theme editor and a review-and-publish flow. WAC is built on all of it. Ripul's own app uses none of it: every font and colour is written at the call site, so "use teal" or "try Archivo" means editing thousands of lines, and nobody can try a look on a phone before deciding.

This plan makes every colour and typeface in the first-party apps come from a theme, without changing how anything looks. A second, small step then applies the brand as a theme document that can be switched on a phone.

## What exists today

Measured on `main`, 10 October 2026.

| Surface | State |
|---|---|
| SDK theme engine | 19 files, about 6,100 lines: three tiers of colour tokens, named styles, remote document with cache and bundle fallback, editor, review and publish, View Explorer readout, label and tab-title text overrides |
| WAC | Registers a vocabulary (`WACThemeSpec.make()`), 47 files and about 220 call sites read tokens, theme document served from `llm-proxy.ripul.io/v1/app-themes/wac-v1` |
| Ripul app | Configures the engine only in a UI-test fixture (`iOS/RipulAppApp.swift:289`). `AccentColor` is an empty asset, so the accent is system blue |
| SDK's own screens | Read no tokens. One file checks whether a theme exists (`Sessions/RipulSolutionsScreen.swift:389`) |
| Web chat | Seven MUI themes and a theming guide, but the themes set no font family (so Roboto), and `src` holds about 2,060 hex literals, 2,000 `rgba(` literals and 790 `fontFamily` values outside the theme files |
| Website | The palette and the two faces as CSS variables in `website/public/css/site.css` |

Native call sites that set a font or a colour directly:

| Directory | Files | Fonts | Named colours | Accent or tint | `.primary`/`.secondary` | System backgrounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ripul-native-app/iOS` | 131 | 556 | 143 | 83 | 374 | 84 |
| `ripul-native-app/Shared` | 86 | 133 | 23 | 9 | 128 | 3 |
| `ripul-native-app/macOS` | 125 | 204 | 30 | 18 | 143 | 11 |
| `ripul-ios-sdk/Sources/RipulAgent` (all) | 447 | 1,366 | 268 | 186 | 1,042 | 138 |

Of the font calls in the iPhone app and SDK, about 1,530 use a text style (`.body`, `.caption`) and about 400 use a fixed size. The first kind can be rewritten by a script. The second kind, the named colours and the backgrounds need a decision each: about 1,100 sites.

### Three gaps in the engine

The engine was lifted from WAC, and WAC is a light-only UIKit app.

1. **No fonts.** The engine resolves colours and style knobs. WAC keeps its font family in its own part of the document and reads it with its own helper (`Font.theme`, `UIFont.themeFontName`).
2. **One value per colour.** A primitive is a single hex. There is no light and dark pair and no way to name a system colour. WAC sets `UIUserInterfaceStyle` to `Light`. Ripul follows the system appearance.
3. **UIKit only.** `ThemeEngine.swift` is inside `#if os(iOS)` and returns `UIColor`. SwiftUI gets a refresh modifier and a themed text view, but no colour or font a view can read. The SDK also builds for macOS 14, where none of this compiles.

A fourth point is structural: the engine holds one vocabulary per process, the host's. The SDK's screens are shown inside WAC as well as inside Ripul, so they cannot read tokens that only Ripul's app registers.

## Decisions

### 1. The first theme is today's look, exactly

The default values of every token are what the code does now: the system font at the system sizes, the system accent, the system backgrounds. A migrated call site therefore renders the same pixels as before. This is what lets many agents land small commits on `main` in any order, and it gives one acceptance test for the whole migration: nothing changed.

It needs two things from the engine. A colour must be able to name a system colour (`system:label`, `system:systemBackground`, `system:tint`) and resolve to the live dynamic colour, so light, dark and increased contrast stay exact. A type role whose family is `system` must return the system text style itself (`Font.body`), not a custom font that resembles it.

### 2. The brand is a second document, applied last

Teal, Archivo and the serif arrive as a theme document after the migration is done, switchable from the theme editor on a phone. The questions argued in the chat that led to this plan (system font or Archivo, blue or teal, neutral canvas or paper) become settings to look at, not decisions to make first.

### 3. A small vocabulary, named for the job

Tokens are named for what they are for, never for their value. The list is in "The vocabulary" below. A leaf agent that needs a token the list lacks does not invent one: it asks the foundation owner, who adds it or names the existing one.

### 4. The SDK owns a base vocabulary beside the host's

The SDK registers its own tokens under a reserved `ripul.` prefix, with defaults in code that give the system look. They resolve in any host, with or without a host theme. Ripul's app supplies a document that overrides them. WAC's vocabulary and document are untouched, and its `Theme.json` stays valid byte for byte.

### 5. Shared places before call sites

A root modifier, the sheet wrapper (`ripulSheet`), the hosting controllers (24 of them), the glass helpers and the shared row components are fixed first. If SwiftUI carries a root foreground style and tint down to `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tint` and `Color.accentColor`, about 1,700 call sites need no edit at all. The foundation proves or disproves that with tests before any leaf work starts (see F3).

### 6. One document for native and web

The chat is a web view inside the native app, so the two must agree. The theme is one JSON document in the repository. The native app bundles it and the web build reads the same file to make the first-party MUI theme. Site-key customers keep their own themes: the first-party theme applies only under the first-party presentation (`config/chatPresentation.ts`).

### 7. A check whose count only falls

A script counts direct fonts and colours per file and compares with a committed baseline. A count above the baseline fails the build. Agents lower the baseline as they migrate. This stops the tree refilling behind them, and its total is the progress measure. `scripts/check_sheet_sizing.py` is the model: it already runs as a pre-build step.

### 8. What is exempt

Some colours and sizes are not theme. They stay, marked with `// theme-exempt: <reason>` so the check can count them apart:

- SF Symbol sizes. A font on an `Image` is an icon size, not type.
- Colours that are data: a provider's or model's colour, a chat's colour, terminal ANSI colours, syntax and diff colours.
- Brand marks: the Claude and Codex marks, the wordmark's lime dot.
- System materials and glass.
- Views that exist only in `#if DEBUG` harnesses.
- Customer content: `CmsRender/` in the SDK and `src/cms` on the web follow the customer's portal theme (`CmsPortalTheme`), not Ripul's.

| `onAccent` | white | Text and icons on an accent fill |
| `canvas` | `system:systemBackground` | The app's background |
| `surface` | `system:secondarySystemGroupedBackground` | Cards and grouped rows |
| `surfaceSunken` | `system:systemGroupedBackground` | The ground behind cards |
| `text` | `system:label` | Primary text |
| `textSecondary` | `system:secondaryLabel` | Detail lines |
| `textTertiary` | `system:tertiaryLabel` | Timestamps, hints |
| `separator` | `system:separator` | Hairlines |

2. Foundation: F1 to F6 and W1, two agents in parallel.

5. Verification across all reference screens, and the live-switch test.

# A theme-aware codebase

**Status**: draft for review, 10 October 2026. Nothing is built.
**Depends on**: the SDK theme engine (shipped, SDK 0.5.10 onward), `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/remote-themes.md`
**Reference host**: `WAC_ios_final` (branch `v3`), the one app built on the engine today

## Problem

Ripul's website has a brand: a warm paper canvas, navy ink, a teal accent, Archivo for text and Instrument Serif for headings. Ripul's apps do not carry it. The native screens are stock iOS (system font, system blue), the chat is Material (Roboto, blue `#0078d4`), and the one branded screen, the empty chat, sits between them looking like a page from the website.

The cause is not taste, it is plumbing. The SDK has a theme engine, a hosted theme document, an in-app theme editor and a review-and-publish flow. WAC is built on all of it. Ripul's own app uses none of it: every font and colour is written at the call site, so "use teal" or "try Archivo" means editing thousands of lines, and nobody can try a look on a phone before deciding.

This plan makes every colour and typeface in the first-party apps come from a theme, without changing how anything looks. A second, small step then applies the brand as a theme document that can be switched on a phone.

## What exists today

Measured on `main`, 10 October 2026.

| Surface | State |
|---|---|
| SDK theme engine | 19 files, about 6,100 lines: three tiers of colour tokens, named styles, remote document with cache and bundle fallback, editor, review and publish, View Explorer readout, label and tab-title text overrides |
| WAC | Registers a vocabulary (`WACThemeSpec.make()`), 47 files and about 220 call sites read tokens, theme document served from `llm-proxy.ripul.io/v1/app-themes/wac-v1` |
| Ripul app | Configures the engine only in a UI-test fixture (`iOS/RipulAppApp.swift:289`). `AccentColor` is an empty asset, so the accent is system blue |
| SDK's own screens | Read no tokens. One file checks whether a theme exists (`Sessions/RipulSolutionsScreen.swift:389`) |
| Web chat | Seven MUI themes and a theming guide, but the themes set no font family (so Roboto), and `src` holds about 2,060 hex literals, 2,000 `rgba(` literals and 790 `fontFamily` values outside the theme files |
| Website | The palette and the two faces as CSS variables in `website/public/css/site.css` |

Native call sites that set a font or a colour directly:

| Directory | Files | Fonts | Named colours | Accent or tint | `.primary`/`.secondary` | System backgrounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ripul-native-app/iOS` | 131 | 556 | 143 | 83 | 374 | 84 |
| `ripul-native-app/Shared` | 86 | 133 | 23 | 9 | 128 | 3 |
| `ripul-native-app/macOS` | 125 | 204 | 30 | 18 | 143 | 11 |
| `ripul-ios-sdk/Sources/RipulAgent` (all) | 447 | 1,366 | 268 | 186 | 1,042 | 138 |

Of the font calls in the iPhone app and SDK, about 1,530 use a text style (`.body`, `.caption`) and about 400 use a fixed size. The first kind can be rewritten by a script. The second kind, the named colours and the backgrounds need a decision each: about 1,100 sites.

### Three gaps in the engine

The engine was lifted from WAC, and WAC is a light-only UIKit app.

1. **No fonts.** The engine resolves colours and style knobs. WAC keeps its font family in its own part of the document and reads it with its own helper (`Font.theme`, `UIFont.themeFontName`).
2. **One value per colour.** A primitive is a single hex. There is no light and dark pair and no way to name a system colour. WAC sets `UIUserInterfaceStyle` to `Light`. Ripul follows the system appearance.
3. **UIKit only.** `ThemeEngine.swift` is inside `#if os(iOS)` and returns `UIColor`. SwiftUI gets a refresh modifier and a themed text view, but no colour or font a view can read. The SDK also builds for macOS 14, where none of this compiles.

A fourth point is structural: the engine holds one vocabulary per process, the host's. The SDK's screens are shown inside WAC as well as inside Ripul, so they cannot read tokens that only Ripul's app registers.

## Decisions

### 1. The first theme is today's look, exactly

The default values of every token are what the code does now: the system font at the system sizes, the system accent, the system backgrounds. A migrated call site therefore renders the same pixels as before. This is what lets many agents land small commits on `main` in any order, and it gives one acceptance test for the whole migration: nothing changed.

It needs two things from the engine. A colour must be able to name a system colour (`system:label`, `system:systemBackground`, `system:tint`) and resolve to the live dynamic colour, so light, dark and increased contrast stay exact. A type role whose family is `system` must return the system text style itself (`Font.body`), not a custom font that resembles it.

### 2. The brand is a second document, applied last

Teal, Archivo and the serif arrive as a theme document after the migration is done, switchable from the theme editor on a phone. The questions argued in the chat that led to this plan (system font or Archivo, blue or teal, neutral canvas or paper) become settings to look at, not decisions to make first.

### 3. A small vocabulary, named for the job

Tokens are named for what they are for, never for their value. The list is in "The vocabulary" below. A leaf agent that needs a token the list lacks does not invent one: it asks the foundation owner, who adds it or names the existing one.

### 4. The SDK owns a base vocabulary beside the host's

The SDK registers its own tokens under a reserved `ripul.` prefix, with defaults in code that give the system look. They resolve in any host, with or without a host theme. Ripul's app supplies a document that overrides them. WAC's vocabulary and document are untouched, and its `Theme.json` stays valid byte for byte.

### 5. Shared places before call sites

A root modifier, the sheet wrapper (`ripulSheet`), the hosting controllers (24 of them), the glass helpers and the shared row components are fixed first. If SwiftUI carries a root foreground style and tint down to `.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tint` and `Color.accentColor`, about 1,700 call sites need no edit at all. The foundation proves or disproves that with tests before any leaf work starts (see F3).

### 6. One document for native and web

The chat is a web view inside the native app, so the two must agree. The theme is one JSON document in the repository. The native app bundles it and the web build reads the same file to make the first-party MUI theme. Site-key customers keep their own themes: the first-party theme applies only under the first-party presentation (`config/chatPresentation.ts`).

### 7. A check whose count only falls

A script counts direct fonts and colours per file and compares with a committed baseline. A count above the baseline fails the build. Agents lower the baseline as they migrate. This stops the tree refilling behind them, and its total is the progress measure. `scripts/check_sheet_sizing.py` is the model: it already runs as a pre-build step.

### 8. What is exempt

Some colours and sizes are not theme. They stay, marked with `// theme-exempt: <reason>` so the check can count them apart:

- SF Symbol sizes. A font on an `Image` is an icon size, not type.
- Colours that are data: a provider's or model's colour, a chat's colour, terminal ANSI colours, syntax and diff colours.
- Brand marks: the Claude and Codex marks, the wordmark's lime dot.
- System materials and glass.
- Views that exist only in `#if DEBUG` harnesses.
- Customer content: `CmsRender/` in the SDK and `src/cms` on the web follow the customer's portal theme (`CmsPortalTheme`), not Ripul's.

## The vocabulary

Proposed. F1 fixes the final names in `ripul-ios-sdk/docs/theming.md`, and that file is what leaf agents read.

Colour roles, each with a light and a dark value:

| Role | Default (today's look) | For |
|---|---|---|
| `accent` | `system:tint` | Selection, links, primary buttons, the unread mark |
| `onAccent` | white | Text and icons on an accent fill |
| `canvas` | `system:systemBackground` | The app's background |
| `surface` | `system:secondarySystemGroupedBackground` | Cards and grouped rows |
| `surfaceSunken` | `system:systemGroupedBackground` | The ground behind cards |
| `text` | `system:label` | Primary text |
| `textSecondary` | `system:secondaryLabel` | Detail lines |
| `textTertiary` | `system:tertiaryLabel` | Timestamps, hints |
| `separator` | `system:separator` | Hairlines |
| `success` | `system:systemGreen` | Online, done |
| `warning` | `system:systemOrange` | Waiting, caution |
| `danger` | `system:systemRed` | Errors, destructive actions |

Type roles. Each has a family, a size, a weight, the text style it scales with, and tracking:

| Role | Default |
|---|---|
| `largeTitle`, `title`, `title2`, `title3`, `headline`, `body`, `callout`, `subheadline`, `footnote`, `caption`, `caption2` | The system text style of the same name |
| `display` | `title` in the system font. The brand theme makes it the serif |
| `eyebrow` | `subheadline`, semibold, uppercase: today's section header |
| `code` | The system monospaced face |

Three families are named in the document: `text`, `display` and `code`. A role may carry a second size for Mac Catalyst, which has no Dynamic Type and where the sidebar already uses fixed 14 and 12 point text (`SidebarRowMetrics`).

Corner radii and spacing are not in this plan (see Open questions).

## Foundation

These land before any leaf work. F1 to F5 are one agent's work in the SDK and app. W1 is a second agent's work on the web. The two do not share files.

**F1. Engine.** Light and dark pairs and `system:` references for colours. Font tokens: families, roles, Dynamic Type. The resolution core compiles on macOS; only the repaint walker and UIKit tagging stay behind `#if os(iOS)`. The base vocabulary of decision 4. All additive: an existing document with hex-only colours and no fonts must load unchanged, and the seven existing theme test files must pass.

**F2. Accessors.** What a view writes. Proposed: `Color.ripul(.accent)`, `Font.ripul(.body)`, `Font.ripul(.caption, weight: .semibold)`, `Font.ripul(size: 14, weight: .medium)` for a fixed size in the theme's family, an icon-size helper for symbols, and UIKit equivalents. A unit test asserts that with the default document each accessor equals the system value it replaces (`Font.ripul(.body) == Font.body`). That test is the proof of decision 1.

**F3. Roots.** A `ripulThemeRoot()` modifier that sets tint, foreground style and default font and refreshes on theme change, applied at both `WindowGroup`s, inside `ripulSheet`, and in the hosting controllers. Tests that answer, for a window, a sheet, a popover and a hosting controller: do `.secondary`, `.tint` and `Color.accentColor` follow the root? The answers go in `theming.md` as the rule leaf agents follow. Where the answer is no, those call sites join the leaf work.

**F4. Ripul's document.** One JSON file at a path both builds can read, registered by the app at launch. With the default values it is nearly empty. The Solutions screen then shows the theme editor for Ripul's own theme.

**F5. The check and the rewrite script.** `ripul-native-app/scripts/check_theme_tokens.py` with its baseline, wired into the pre-build steps beside the sheet check. A rewrite script for the mechanical cases (`.font(.body)` and its `.weight`, `.bold()`, `.monospacedDigit()` forms), which leaf agents run on their own files.

**F6. Reference screens.** A script that puts the simulator into a fixed state (launch arguments and fixture data, as the UI tests do), captures about a dozen screens in light and dark, and reports a pixel difference per screen as text. Run once before leaf work to make the baseline.

**W1. Web foundation.**
- Give the theme a `text`, `display` and `code` family and move the first-party font choices into it (today: Roboto by default, `'Segoe UI', Roboto` for tool calls in `chatPresentation.ts`, the serif inside `V2StarterScreen.tsx`).
- Generate the first-party light and dark MUI themes from the shared document, with today's values as the default.
- List which `src` directories the first-party apps actually render. This decides W4's scope.
- A literals check with a per-directory baseline, the web twin of F5.
- A computed-style snapshot: a script run through the browser tools that records font and colour for every `data-ui` element on the reference pages, as JSON, for before-and-after comparison.

The foundation ends with a WAC compile against the new SDK, to confirm nothing WAC uses has changed.

## Workstreams

After the foundation, each stream owns a set of files and edits nothing outside it. Sizes are the number of lines that set a font or colour. Streams can be combined; the ownership boundaries are what matter.

| Stream | Owns | Files | Sites |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | `ripul-ios-sdk/Sources/RipulAgent/Sessions/` | 82 | 585 |
| S2 | SDK top-level files A to M | 87 | 280 |
| S3 | SDK top-level files N to S | 62 | 412 |
| S4 | SDK top-level files T to Z | 28 | 285 |
| S5 | SDK subdirectories other than `Sessions/` and `CmsRender/` (`Speech`, `Macros`, `PlanReview`, `ToolRenderers`, `ToolCollections` and the rest) | about 130 | about 410 fonts |
| A1 | `ripul-native-app/iOS/` files A to L | 51 | 382 |
| A2 | `ripul-native-app/iOS/` files M to R | 44 | 432 |
| A3 | `ripul-native-app/iOS/` files S to Z | 34 | 277 |
| A4 | `ripul-native-app/Shared/`, `RipulWidgets/`, `Browser/` | 73 | about 290 |
| W2 | `chrome-extension/src/logging/components/chat/` | | 277 hex, 40 font families |
| W3 | `chrome-extension/src/logging/panels/` | | 200 hex, 251 font families (mostly `monospace`) |
| W4 | The other directories W1 lists as shown in the first-party apps | | set by W1 |

S1 goes first among the native streams: it holds the session list and the rows, the screens this plan started from, and it will find the gaps in the accessors while only one agent is affected.

The widgets in A4 run in their own process and cannot read the live engine. They read the bundled document.

What each native stream does, in order:

1. Run the rewrite script on its files. Commit.
2. Fixed-size fonts on text: `Font.ripul(size:weight:)`. On an image: the icon helper.
3. Named colours: a role where the colour means something (green for online is `success`), an exemption where it is data.
4. System backgrounds: `canvas`, `surface` or `surfaceSunken`.
5. Raw RGB values: a role, or a request to the foundation owner for a new token.
6. Lower the baseline for its files. Commit.

| Today | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `.font(.body)` | `.font(.ripul(.body))` |
| `.font(.caption.weight(.semibold))` | `.font(.ripul(.caption, weight: .semibold))` |
| `.font(.system(size: 14, weight: .medium))` on text | `.font(.ripul(size: 14, weight: .medium))` |
| `.font(.system(size: 18))` on `Image(systemName:)` | the icon-size helper |
| `Color.blue` used as the accent | `Color.ripul(.accent)` |
| `Color.green` for online or done | `Color.ripul(.success)` |
| `Color(.systemBackground)` | `Color.ripul(.canvas)` |
| `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, `.tint`, `Color.accentColor` | unchanged if F3 proves the root reaches them; otherwise the matching role |

On the web, colour literals become theme tokens as the theming guide already requires, `rgba(` literals become `alpha()` of a palette value, and `fontFamily` values become the theme's `text` or `code` family or are removed so the element inherits. Font sizes stay as they are: `uiScale` already scales them, and they are not part of this plan.

## Rules for every agent

- **Files.** Edit only your stream's files. A change you need elsewhere goes to that file's owner, or to the foundation owner for anything in the accessors or the vocabulary.
- **No visual change.** A migration commit must not change what a screen looks like. If the faithful mapping looks wrong (an 8 point label, two greens that differ), keep it faithful and add it to the list in "The brand theme". Fixing looks is a later step.
- **Commits.** Small, on `main`, pushed at once, as `CLAUDE.md` requires. One directory or one screen per commit.
- **Builds.** Native builds share one train lane, so they queue. Compile-check SDK work with `swift build --scratch-path /tmp/ripul-theme-<stream>` and use the simulator train (`ship_duo_sim.py`) only at the end of the stream. Never a new DerivedData path inside the repository.
- **The web.** `npx tsgo --noEmit` after every change. Deploy through the web train, with a hold while comparing snapshots.
- **Unsure.** Record a comment on this plan against the stream's section. Do not guess a token.

## Verification

- **By construction.** The accessor test (F2) proves each default equals the system value, and the rewrite script changes syntax only.
- **The check.** The baseline total for in-scope directories reaches zero, exemptions listed apart.
- **Reference screens.** The pixel difference against the F6 baseline is zero, or explained, after each native stream. One agent runs this per stream, not per commit.
- **Web snapshots.** The computed-style JSON for the reference pages is unchanged after each web stream.
- **Compatibility.** Existing theme tests pass. WAC compiles against the SDK and its theme loads unchanged.
- **Live switch.** With everything migrated, loading a document that sets the accent to magenta and the text family to a serif changes every reference screen. A screen that does not change has a call site the check missed.

## The brand theme

After the migration. One agent, then Peter on a phone.

- Bundle the fonts natively: Archivo and Instrument Serif. The website has only `woff2` files; the app needs the source `ttf` files (both are under the Open Font License).
- Write the brand document: `accent` teal `#1f6f70` light and `#62b9b4` dark, the `text` family Archivo, the `display` family Instrument Serif, `eyebrow` with the website's letter-spacing.
- Generate the web themes from it. The three other teals in the chat (`#00897B`, `#4a90a4`, `#40e0d0`) become the accent, and the empty chat's four dot colours become one.

- Publish it as a hosted theme (`ripul-v1`) so it can change without a release.
- Settle the items leaf agents listed. Known so far: the tool label under a session row's icon is fixed at 8 points (`UnifiedSessionRow.swift:397`); the model name in each row is drawn in the provider's colour.
- Redraw the phones on the website to match the app.

## Out of scope

- The Mac host (`ripul-native-app/macOS`, 125 files). It must keep compiling, since `Shared/` and the SDK build for it, but its screens are not migrated here.
- Customer-themed content: `CmsRender/`, `src/cms`, site-key themes, `src/content-injection`.
- Web surfaces the first-party apps do not show (admin, forms, the workflow designer). They stay under the check's baseline and fall as they are touched.
- Web font sizes, corner radii, spacing.
- Moving WAC's fonts onto the new font tokens. It becomes possible; it is WAC's own change.

## Order

1. This plan is reviewed and locked.
2. Foundation: F1 to F6 and W1, two agents in parallel.
3. S1 alone, to shake out the accessors.
4. The remaining streams in parallel: up to eight native and three web.
5. Verification across all reference screens, and the live-switch test.
6. The brand theme.

1. **Canvas.** Does the brand theme keep the neutral system canvas, or take the website's paper and navy? Recommendation: neutral first, and try paper as a variant once it is one setting.
2. **Main or worktrees.** Recommendation: `main`, because commits change nothing visible, files do not overlap, and the trains build from `main`. A worktree per stream would mean cold builds and a merge at the end.
3. **The SDK's screens inside WAC.** Stay on the system look, or follow WAC's theme? Recommendation: system look by default; a host may override the `ripul.` tokens later.
4. **How far into the web.** Recommendation: what the first-party apps show now, the rest under the check with no date.

content.text:
The plan is written, committed and pushed: `docs/plans/theme-aware-codebase.md`, with 16 tasks in the Plans screen. (The voice session dropped partway through, so this is written.)

**The core idea:** the first theme is today's look exactly. Every token defaults to what the code does now, so a migrated line renders the same pixels and agents can land small commits on `main` in any order. The brand (teal, Archivo, the serif) is then a second theme document applied at the end, which you can switch on your phone.

**Scale, native app and SDK:**
- About 1,530 font calls are mechanical and a script rewrites them.
- About 1,100 sites need a decision each (fixed sizes, named colours, backgrounds).
- About 1,700 more (`.secondary`, tint, accent) may need no edit if one root modifier reaches them. The foundation tests that before anything else is sized.

**Gaps the plan has to close in the SDK first:**
- The engine has no fonts.
- It holds one value per colour, with no light and dark pair, because WAC is light-only.
- It is UIKit-only and does not compile for macOS.
- The SDK's own screens also show inside WAC, so they need a base set of tokens that does not depend on Ripul's app.

**Order:**
1. Foundation, two agents in parallel: one on the SDK and app, one on the web.
2. One agent migrates the session list alone, to shake out the new API.
3. The remaining streams in parallel, up to eight native and three web. Each owns a set of files, split by directory and alphabetically, so none overlap.
4. A verification pass, then the brand theme.

Only the two foundation agents can start now; the rest have nothing to write against until that lands.

**Your call before spawning** (the plan has six open questions, each with my recommendation; these two change how the agents are set up):
- **`main` or worktrees:** I recommend `main`, because the commits change nothing visible, the files don't overlap and the trains build from `main`. Worktrees would mean cold builds and a merge at the end.
- **How far into the web:** I recommend only what the first-party apps show, with admin, forms and the workflow designer left under a check that stops them getting worse. I have not yet confirmed which web directories those apps render; that is the web foundation's first job.

The plan shows as Locked only because nobody has reviewed it yet. A review pass by another agent before the foundation starts would be cheap.

{"guide":"# Working inside Ripul

You are a coding agent running inside Ripul Host, an app on the user's Mac. The user may be at the Mac, or driving this chat from an iPhone or another Mac, and other agents may be working on the same repository at the same time.

## Your process can end between turns

Ripul keeps one long-lived agent process per chat, so most turns continue in the same process. It still ends that process, and every child process with it, when:

- Ripul Host is restarted or updated;
- the user changes the model or the reasoning effort for the chat;
- the user switches account, or rewinds the chat;
- the chat has produced no output for about half an hour and other chats need the memory (a chat with a job still running is left alone).

The next turn resumes the conversation in a new process. The conversation survives; anything the old process was running does not.

So a job that takes more than a few minutes must not be a child of your process. Do not rely on a background task or a monitor for it. Start it detached and read a log:

```bash
nohup bash -c 'cd /path/to/project && ./long-job.sh; echo "EXIT_CODE=$?"' > /tmp/long-job.log 2>&1 &
disown
tail -n 20 /tmp/long-job.log    # later, as often as you need
```

Change directory inside the detached command, and look at the first lines of the log straight away: a bad launch fails within a second.

## A commit also saves this chat

In a Claude chat, each `git commit` you make leaves a copy of the chat's transcript on a branch named `claude-sessions` in the same repository, pushed to its remote, so the chat can be continued on another Mac. Ripul does this through a git hooks directory it sets for your process. `git config core.hooksPath` showing a folder under `~/.ripul/session-capture` is that, not a fault: leave it. The repository's own hooks still run.

Two things follow. Anything you printed in this chat, including a secret that appeared in a command's output, goes where the repository goes. And a commit you make in some other repository sends this chat's transcript to that repository.

## Asking the user

Ask through the question tool Ripul gives you (`ask_user`, from the `ripul_permissions` server): the user sees a card with your options, on whichever device they are using. A question tool of your own that needs a terminal will not reach them. If nobody answers within a few minutes the call returns unanswered: carry on with the safest choice and say what you assumed.

## Spoken messages

A message wrapped in `<voice>` was spoken, and the user is listening, not reading. Answer with the speak tool named in the note that comes with the message: one to three short sentences, no lists, paths or code. Put the detail in your written reply, which stays on screen. If the speak tool reports that nothing was spoken, the call has ended: answer in writing.

## Ripul's tools

Ripul's tools come from the `ripul_tools` server. Their names say where they act: `host_…` on the Mac running Ripul Host, `device_…` on a connected phone, tablet or simulator, `browser_…` in Ripul's browser. Your client may list them by name only until you look one up.

## What agents learn about a repository

When a repository has a `.ripul/memories/` folder, that is where its agents' memories live, and it is tracked in git with the code. Save what you learn about the repository there, and commit it with the work.
